Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
ECOLOGICAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT
Introduction
This section presents the baseline ecological profile of the Assessment Area, and the
assessment of potential ecological impacts resulting from the construction and
operation of the Project. The location plan and description of the Project are
presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 2.1 and Chapter 2 respectively. In terms of
ECR Alignment and its design, considerable thought went into selecting the most
appropriate option from environmental and engineering perspectives as detailed in
Section 2.5 and Section 2.6. For the purpose of the ecological impact assessment,
two spatial boundaries are defined as:
• Project Boundary: refers to the entire project area, including areas resumed for
the Project that would not be subject to any construction works
• Construction Area of the Project: refers to all areas will be directly impacted by
the project construction works.
According to the Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment
Process (EIAO-TM), baseline conditions for ecological components of the
environment were evaluated based on available literature and field surveys
conducted for the purposes of this Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA).
Measures required to mitigate any identified adverse impacts are recommended,
where appropriate, and residual impacts are addressed.
Environmental Legislation, Standards and Guidelines
This report makes reference to the following HKSAR Government ordinances,
regulations, standards, guidelines, and documents where identifying ecological
importance of habitats and species, and evaluating and assessing potential
ecological impacts of the Project:-
• EIA Study Brief (ESB-375/2025) issued for the proposed project, Development
of the Loop – Eastern Connection Road
• Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance (EIAO) (Cap. 499) and
subsidiary legislation and guidelines
• EIAO Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process
(EIAO-TM) Annexes 8 and 16
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 3/2010 - Flexibility and Enforceability of Mitigation
Measures Proposed in an Environmental Impact Assessment Report
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 6/2010 - Some Observations on Ecological
Assessment from the Environmental Impact Assessment Ordinance
Perspective
• EIAO Guidance Note No. 7/2010 – Ecological Baseline Survey for Ecological
Assessment

Assessment Methodology
Assessment Area
In accordance with the EIA Study Brief No. ESB-375/2025, the Assessment Area for
the purpose of the terrestrial and aquatic ecological impact assessment includes
areas within 500m from the Project Boundary of the Project and associated works,
as well as other areas likely to be impacted by the Project (60722948/A10/FIGURE
8.1 refers).
Literature Review
A literature review was conducted including ecological information from previous EIA
reports, published academic studies, relevant grey literature and relevant EM&A data.
These sources provided a basis for understanding the ecological context of the
Assessment Area.
Ecological Survey Methodology
In agreement with relevant authorities and following the ecological survey
requirements described in Appendix G in the EIA Study Brief, ecological surveys were
undertaken from July 2022 to December 2023 (Table 8.1 refers), covering both the
wet and dry seasons. The purpose of the ecological surveys was to verify the
information from literature review, collect up-to-date ecological baseline information
and fill information gaps. This facilitates subsequent assessment of ecological value,
evaluation of the potential ecological impacts resulting from the Project, and provision
of appropriate mitigation measures. Survey transects for habitat, vegetation,
mammals, avifauna, herpetofauna, butterflies, odonates and fireflies; and sampling
points for aquatic fauna, camera traps and flight-line surveys; are shown in
60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2.
In response to the amendments to EIAO and the revision of the EIAO-TM (introduced
in April 2023) during the 12-month ecological survey programme undertaken for this
Project, additional freshwater fish and firefly surveys (Table 8.1) were conducted to
meet the latest EIAO-TM requirements. The ecologists and other personnel with
relevant experience who led and conducted the surveys are summarised in
Appendix 8.1.
The recommended timing and methodology of surveys for specific taxa followed the
EIAO GN No. 7/2023 and No. 10/2023. Survey methodologies for habitats/vegetation
and different faunal groups are described in the following sections.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Habitat and vegetation surveys of the Assessment Area were undertaken in July and
November (2022) and in March and June (2023), covering both dry and wet seasons.
Habitats were identified, sized and mapped based on recent aerial photos and field
ground-truthing. Habitats were characterised and defined with reference to size,
vegetation type, flora species present, dominant species, species diversity and
abundance, community structure and seasonality, as well as the presence of any
features of ecological importance. Representative colour photos were taken for each
habitat type and any important ecological features identified. Habitat maps of suitable
scale were prepared.
Vegetation surveys were conducted within each habitat type by direct observation.
Plant species from each habitat type were identified and their relative abundance
recorded. The location of any plant species of conservation importance (e.g. Incense
Tree, Aquilaria sinensis) was recorded. Nomenclature of plant species follows the
latest Hong Kong Plant Database (HKPD) available from the website of the Hong
Kong Herbarium (AFCD, 2021).
Avifauna
Daytime and nighttime bird surveys were carried out on a monthly basis from July
2022 to June 2023, covering dry and wet seasons. Daytime surveys were carried out
in the early morning at the period of peak bird activity, while night surveys were
conducted after dusk to record nocturnal avifauna. The bird communities of each
habitat type within the Assessment Area were surveyed along survey transects
(60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2 refers). All birds seen or heard along the survey
transects were counted and identified to species where possible. The location and
nature of any substantial waterbird foraging and roosting sites were recorded. Signs
of breeding (e.g. nests and/ or recently fledged juveniles) within the Assessment Area,
especially within the Construction Area of the Project, were also recorded and
mapped. Surveyors used 7X to 10X binoculars and/or a 30X to 65X spotting scope
mounted on tripod for the surveys and photographic records. Ornithological
nomenclature follows the latest List of Hong Kong Birds (HKBWS, 2024).
Specific surveys of the flight-line and flight behaviour of waterbirds and other larger
avifauna species of conservation importance within the Hoo Hok Wai (HHW) wetland
areas were undertaken in early morning during peak periods of bird activity (from
November 2022 to February 2023; and from May to June 2023). The flight-line
surveys were undertaken at two vantage points simultaneously and continuously for
two hours. The bird species, direction and height of flight adopted were recorded. The
location of the vantage points is shown in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2.
Mammals
A total of seven camera traps were deployed throughout the Assessment Area at
secure and appropriate locations subject to the agreement of the lease owners
(60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2 refers) to survey cryptic non-flying terrestrial mammals,
focusing on areas with potential mammal usage. Monthly mammal surveys (including
day and night-time surveys, covering the dry and wet seasons) were carried out from
July 2022 to June 2023. As most mammals occur in low densities, tracks and signs
of mammals (e.g. droppings) were actively searched for (as well as direct sightings)
along the survey transects (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2). Dusk and night surveys
were conducted to survey nocturnal mammal species (e.g. rodents and bats).

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Particular attention was given to searching for Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra)’s holts in
potential suitable habitats such as terrestrial areas adjacent to water bodies (Shek,
2006). Active search for field signs of otter (including but not limited to spraints,
footprints, scratch marks, etc) across the Assessment Area were conducted. In
addition, camera traps were deployed at locations considered to be potential
Eurasian Otter activity areas.
Bat surveys were conducted at dusk through direct observations and using a bat
detector. Particular attention was given to potential foraging and drinking sites such
as fruiting trees and freshwater ponds (Tong, 2016). All bat calls recorded were
identified according to species-specific echolocation call structure (Tong, 2016).
All mammals seen during the survey were counted and identified to species where
possible. Nomenclature for mammals follows that the Hong Kong Biodiversity
Information Hub (AFCD, 2024c).
Herpetofauna
Daytime and nighttime herpetofauna surveys were carried out from July to October
2022 and from March to June 2023, covering the dry and wet seasons. Herpetofauna
surveys were conducted through direct observation in all habitat types along the
survey transects (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2 refers) and active searching of hiding
places such as among leaf litter, inside holes, under stones and logs. Particular
attention was given to streams and other water features. In addition to visual surveys,
auditory detection of species-specific calls was used to survey frogs and toads.
During the surveys, all reptiles and amphibians sighted and heard were counted and
identified, with the location of herpetofauna species with conservation importance
mapped. Special attention was paid to streams and riparian areas in Ma Tso Lung,
where the critically endangered Three-banded Box Turtle (Cuora trifasciata) was
recorded in the reviewed literature, and Tse Koo Hang, which has been identified as
a potential habitat for the Three-banded Box Turtle (Ove Arup, 2013a). Nomenclature
for herpetofauna follows that available from the Hong Kong Biodiversity Information
Hub (HKBIH) (AFCD, 2024c).
Butterflies and Odonates
Daytime butterfly and odonate surveys were carried out from July to November 2022
and from March to June 2023, while odonate surveys were carried out from July to
October 2022 and from April to June 2023. Butterflies and odonates were identified
and counted by direct observation in different habitats within the Assessment Area
along the survey transects (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2). Nomenclature for butterflies
and odonates follows HKBIH (AFCD, 2024).
Fireflies
Monthly firefly surveys were carried out along the survey transects at dusk and night
from April to June 2023 and from October to December 2023. Firefly larvae and adults
were identified to species level where possible. The location of firefly species of
conservation importance or any notable behaviour (e.g. breeding) were recorded.
Nomenclature and conservation status of fireflies follow Yiu (2023).

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Assessment Approach
The criteria and guidelines stated in Annexes 8 and 16 of the EIAO-TM were followed
for evaluating and assessing ecological impacts arising from the construction and
operation of the Project. Potential direct / indirect, on-site / off-site, primary, secondary,
cumulative and residual ecological impacts arising from the construction and
operation of the Project were identified and evaluated where possible. Mitigation
measures and monitoring and audit programme were recommended as required.
Description of the Environment
Recognised Sites of Conservation Importance
The recognised sites of conservation importance identified within the Assessment
Area are shown in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1 and are described below.
Proposed Hoo Hok Wai Wetland Conservation Park (HHW WCP)
The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) has conducted a
Strategic Feasibility Study on the Development of Wetland Conservation Parks
(WCPs) System (hereafter referred as the WCPs System FS), which proposed the
establishment of four new Wetland Conservation Parks (Sam Po Shue WCP, Hong
Kong Wetland Park Expansion Area, Hoo Hok Wai WCP (including Sha Ling / Nam
Hang area), and Nam Sang Wai WCP) across the Northwest New Territories (AFCD,
2024a). The four main objectives of the WCPs System are:
• Conserving the ecological value of the wetlands and safeguarding the integrity
of the wetlands system;
• Developing modernised aquaculture industry to create more job opportunities
for the agriculture and fisheries industries;
• Promoting scientific research on aquaculture to facilitate the upgrading and
transformation of the agriculture and fisheries industries; and
• Providing ecological education and recreational facilities for the public.
While the boundary of the proposed HHW WCP is subject to further review and
confirmation, the proposed park boundary of the HHW WCP (including Sha Ling /
Nam Hang area) is shown in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1, covering approximately
277 ha and comprising managed and unmanaged ponds, marshes and reedbeds, as
well as compensatory wetlands. These habitats support diverse wetland fauna
species, particularly waterbirds and Eurasian Otter. Part of the Project Boundary falls
within the proposed HHW WCP (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1). AFCD (2024a) notes
that the next stage of detailed studies for the WCPs System should take into account
any interface issue with these developments (including the ECR Project) when more
information becomes available.
Wetland Conservation Area (WCA) and Wetland Buffer Area (WBA)
The northwestern part of the Assessment Area falls within the Wetland Conservation
Area (WCA) (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1 refers). The WCA was designated by the
Town Planning Board (TPB) to conserve the ecological value of the fishponds in the
8-8 February 2026

text:
Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Deep Bay wetland ecosystem (TPB Guideline No. 12C – Application for
developments within Deep Bay area under Section 16 of the Town Planning
Ordinance revised in May 2014 by TPB). The WCA comprises the existing and
contiguous active or abandoned fishponds in the Deep Bay Area, which should be
conserved.
New development within the WCA would not be allowed unless it is required to
support the conservation of the ecological value of the area or the development is an
essential infrastructural project with overriding public interest. Any such development
should be supported by an ecological impact assessment to demonstrate that the
development would not result in a net loss in wetland function and negative
disturbance impact.
The central part of the Project Boundary and Assessment Area falls within the
Wetland Buffer Area (WBA, 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1 refers). The WBA is
approximately 500m in width and lies along the landward boundary of the WCA. The
intention of WBA is to protect the ecological integrity of wetland habitats within the
WCA (TPB Guideline No. 12C). Development within the WBA causing negative
impacts on the ecological value of the WCA would not be supported by TPB, unless
an ecological impact assessment can demonstrate that the negative impacts could
be mitigated through positive measures. All works conducted within the WCA and
WBA should comply with the “No-Net-Loss in Wetland” principle. Wetland
compensation is required for any development involving pond filling and mitigation
measures against disturbance would be necessary and would be imposed as part of
the planning approval conditions.
“Conservation Area” (“CA” zone)
Areas zoned “CA” under the Approved LMCL Outline Zoning Plan (OZP) No.
S/LMCL/2, the Approved San Tin Technopole OZP No. S/STT/2 and the Ma Tso Lung
and Hoo Hok Wai Outline Zoning Plan S/NE-MTL/3 fall within the Project Boundary
and Assessment Area (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1).
The Lok Ma Chau (LMC) Meander (also known as Old Shenzhen River Meander) to
the southeast of the Lok Ma Chau Loop (hereinafter referred to as “the Loop”) is
designated as “CA” zone under the Approved LMCL OZP No. S/LMCL/2. The
planning intention of this zone is to protect and retain the existing natural landscape
and ecological features of the LMC Meander and the associated riparian vegetation,
which forms an important element of the flight line corridor for birds and is used by
the Eurasian Otter, for conservation, educational and research purposes, and to
separate sensitive natural environment from the adverse effects of development.
There is a general presumption against development in this zone. In general, only
developments that are needed to support the conservation of the ecological integrity
of the wetland ecosystem or the existing natural landscape or scenic quality of the
LMC Meander or are essential infrastructure projects with overriding public interest
may be permitted.
The “CA” zone under the Approved San Tin Technopole OZP No. S/STT/2 mostly
comprises the existing contiguous and continuous, active or abandoned fishponds to

intention is to discourage new development unless it is required to support the
conservation of the ecological integrity of the wetland ecosystem or the development
is an essential infrastructure project within overriding public interest.
Priority Sites for Enhanced Conservation
The New Nature Conservation Policy (NNCP) of the HKSAR Government identified
twelve priority sites for enhanced conservation. Under the NNCP, two schemes,
namely the Nature Conservation Management Agreement (MA) Scheme and the
Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Scheme, were introduced to enhance the
conservation of ecologically important sites, particularly those on land under private
ownership. (AFCD, 2024d).
One of the twelve sites identified is the ‘Deep Bay Wetland Outside Ramsar Site
Priority Site for Enhanced Conservation’ which falls partly within the Project Boundary
and Assessment Area (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1 refers). The major habitat type of
the Site is pond, which are man-made and intensively modified by humans. The Site
maintains certain characteristics of natural wetland that attract waterbirds and other
wildlife, making it a semi-natural habitat. One hundred and sixty-six bird species,
including the Black-faced Spoonbill (Platalea minor), were recorded therein (AFCD,
2004a). It was ranked 9th among the 12 Priority Sites for Enhanced Conservation.
Other Ecologically Sensitive Resources
Inner Deep Bay and Shenzhen River Catchment Important Bird Area (IBA)
The Inner Deep Bay and Shenzhen River Catchment was identified as an Important
Bird Area (IBA) in 2003 (Birdlife International, 2003). The IBA is an estuarine area
comprising a variety of habitats, including (1) freshwater agricultural lands at Long
Valley; (2) ponds at Ma Tso Lung, Lok Ma Chau, San Tin, Lin Barn Tsuen, Mai Po,

Compensatory Wetlands
“Ecological Area” (“EA”)
Ecological Area (EA) is approximately 12.78ha in size, and is located along the
southeastern edge of the Loop (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1 refers). It was created to
compensate for the loss of wetland habitats (including 10.96ha reed marsh and 0.50
ha of freshwater marsh) as part of the Development of Lok Ma Chau Loop EIA (Ove
Arup, 2013a), hereafter referred to as the LMC Loop EIA. The EA aims to provide an
unfragmented, managed and undisturbed wetland habitat for maximising connectivity
with existing wetland habitats and protecting the flight line corridor. Furthermore, a
50m wide low-rise building buffer zone from the EA, with appropriate screen-planting,
will be established between the EA and developments within the Loop to minimise
disturbance and impacts on avifaunal flight paths from the Loop. The LMC Loop EIA
predicted that birds flying over the Loop area and potentially affected by construction
activities would re-route to fly over LMC Meander and the EA and its buffer zone. The
EA was established in December 2022, and subsequent monitoring of marsh and
reed marsh habitats within the EA have shown it supports a variety of fauna species
of conservation importance, including Greater Painted-snipe (Rostratula
benghalensis), Little Egret (Egretta garzetta), Collared Crow (Corvus torquatus),
Yellow-breasted Bunting (Emberiza aureola), Leopard Cat (Prionailurus bengalensis),
Eurasian Otter, Chinese Bullfrog (Hoplobatrachus rugulosus), Chinese Cobra (Naja
atra) and Ruby Darter (Rhodothemis rufa) (AFCD, unpublished data).
Off-site Wetland Compensation Areas (OWCAs)
Offsite Wetland Compensation Areas (OWCAs) comprise compensatory off-site
wetland areas constructed to mitigate direct, indirect, permanent and temporary
wetland impacts resulting from Development of the Loop, Western Connection Road
(WCR), ECR and Direct Link to LMC Station. The OWCA were proposed in the LMC
Loop EIA (although the ECR was excluded prior to the approval stage of this EIA
report). Three areas of existing pond habitat, comprising Areas 2, 7 and 9, were
proposed as OWCA, with enhancement works at these Areas completed in October
2022. While only one of these (Area 2) falls within the Assessment Area, details of all
three are summarised in Table 8.2 below.
Area 2 is situated to the immediate northeast of the LMC Meander. It is composed of
pond habitat and marsh (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1 refers) to mitigate the
permanent loss of pond and marsh habitat in LMC arising from the construction of
the WCR, permanent loss of pond habitat caused by the construction of the Loop,
and the potential loss of marsh habitat caused by the ECR. According to EM&A
monitoring data (AFCD&CEDD, 2022), Area 2 supports a variety of waterbirds, such
as Chinese Pond Heron (Ardeola bacchus), Little Egret, Great Egret (Ardea alba) and
Grey Heron (Ardea cinerea); raptors, including Black Kite (Milvus migrans), Eastern
Buzzard (Buteo japonicus), Common Kestrel (Falco tinnunculus), and Western
Osprey (Pandion haliaetus); and open-country species, such as Buff-bellied Pipit
(Anthus rubescens), Japanese Quail (Coturnix japonica) and Zitting Cisticola
(Cisticola juncidis).

Habitat and Vegetation
A total of 13 habitat types were previously identified within the Assessment Area,
comprising pond, compensatory wetlands, marsh, reed, modified watercourse, semi-
natural / natural watercourse, seasonally wet grassland, woodland, grassland /
shrubland, orchard, plantation, agricultural land and developed area. Most of these
recorded habitats were also identified within the Construction Area of the Project,
dominated by ponds, grassland/shrubland, seasonally wet grassland and developed
area.
General Description of Habitats within the Assessment Area
An extensive area of mostly active ponds was recorded in HHW, along the northern
part of the Assessment Area. Although vegetation diversity in this habitat was low,
largely limited to common herbaceous species along the pond bunds (Ove Arup,
2013a and 2013b), the ecological value of the ponds was considered of high value,
as they supported a high diversity and abundance of waterbirds and other wetland-
dependent faunal species. The latest published report (WWF, 2025a and 2025b;
Zheng et al, 2023) have been reviewed for ecological impact assessment on the
habitats and species of conservation importance. The ponds in HHW form part of the
identified biodiversity hotspot Inner Deep Bay, which supports the richest birdlife in
Hong Kong and is the only know local breeding site for the Eurasian Otter (WWF,
2025a; 2025b). The area is also recognised for its important ecological connectivity
function (Zheng, 2023). Previous surveys recorded three ponds to the southeast of
the LMC Meander within the Project Boundary, all of which were reported as being
abandoned (Ove Arup, 2013a and 2013b).
Patches of other wetland habitats formed from abandoned ponds/agricultural land
were recorded interspersed with the pond habitats and close to Ma Tso Lung Village.
These included marsh, reedbeds and seasonally wet grassland.
Two areas of compensatory wetland were recorded in the Assessment Area, the EA
and OWCA Area 2. The EA comprises an area of approximately 12.78 ha containing
reed marsh and marsh habitat, support a mix of cultivated floating, emergent and
submerged plants (Ove Arup, 2013a and 2013b). Following establishment and

The hillsides in the south and southeast of the Assessment Area were dominated by

by frequent hillfires (Chan et al., 2023 and 2024). Smaller patches of woodland,
orchard and plantation were recorded from hillside areas, mostly around Ma Tso Lung

Several watercourses were recorded from the Assessment Area, the largest of which
is the LMC Meander which surrounds the Loop. The LMC Meander was originally
part of Shenzhen River before diversion, and was restored to mitigate the loss of
ponds from training of the Shenzhen River (Ove Arup, 2013a). The Ma Tso Lung
Stream flows largely south to north through the Assessment Area, and is in generally
good condition in the upper reaches. The mid-section of the stream (to the northwest
of Ma Tso Lung Village) has been channelised with concrete. The downstream
section of the stream flows into the larger wetland area in HHW.
The majority of the flora species recorded in the Assessment Area were common and
widespread in Hong Kong, and typical of the observed habitats. For instance, the
seasonally wet grassland was occupied by herb species such as Miscanthus sinensis.
Plantation habitat was mainly comprised of exotic tress species such Taiwan Acacia
(Acacia confusa). Fruit trees such as Lychee (Litchi chinensis) and Longan
(Dimocarpus longan) were commonly recorded in habitats including
orchard/developed area. Only one flora species of conservation importance, Incense
Tree was reported from the reviewed literature, recorded in secondary woodland near
Ma Tso Lung (Table 8.6 refers).
Fauna
Faunal diversity (particularly in wetland habitats) was relatively high in the
Assessment Area. A total of 217 faunal species of conservation importance were
noted from the reviewed literature, comprising 169 bird species (Table 8.5 refers),
12 mammal species, 11 herpetofauna species, 14 butterfly species, 9 odonate
species and two aquatic fauna species (Table 8.6 and 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.4
refers).
Avifauna
The Assessment Area comprises a wide array of wetland habitats which were
considered to be significant for avifauna and supported a high diversity of resident

reported being wetland dependent to some extent, including notable species such as
Black-faced Spoonbill, and Eastern Marsh Harrier (Circus spilonotus). The pond

Monitoring Programme (HKBWS, 2018-2023), with Little Egret, Great Cormorant and
Chinese Pond Heron commonly recorded from pond and occasionally recorded from
marsh habitats.

The Loop area and its vicinity are an important flight corridor linking HHW with the
broader Northwestern New Territories (NWNT) wetland area to the southwest.
Morning surveys recorded over 80% of ardeids flying northwards towards HHW and
LMC, with lower usage of 10% toward the Ma Tso Lung. Most flights occurred at low
altitudes (0-10m). Evening surveys showed a similar pattern, with nearly all ardeids
returning from HHW to the roost (AECOM, unpublished).
Ove Arup (2013a) recorded a total of 9,155 bird flight records during surveys
conducted for the LMC Loop EIA, with a clear seasonal pattern observed, whereby
more bird flights were recorded during dry season. The majority of birds in flight were
observed following a main corridor along Ha Wan Tsuen, the LMC Meander, and
towards HHW.
Flight line surveys from areas to the south of LMC Spur Line and San Sham Road to
Hoo Hok Wai were also conducted under the EM&A programme for the LMC Loop
EIA (CEDD, 2023a). The majority of waterbirds notably Great Cormorant, Grey Heron,
Great Egret, Black-faced Spoonbill continued to use this flight corridor (approximately
150m along LMC Meander and 50m along the EA and Shenzhen River). Overall, the
majority of the flight surveys conducted between June 2021 to September 2023
observed more than 50% of monthly recorded birds utilising flight lines of 25m or
above. Usage of flight lines between 15-25m height generally comprised less than
40% monthly records, and usage of flight lines between 10-15m is generally less than
5% usage. Seasonal and inter-year fluctuations were also observed, with usage of
higher flight lines (25m or above) recorded during November to March of 2022
compared to 2021.
Nursery / Breeding Ground
The literature review recorded no notable nursery and breeding behaviour from the
Project Boundary. However, Ove Arup (2013a and 2013b) reported that Eurasian
Eagle Owl (Bubo bubo) is presumed to breed in the more extensive areas of
grassland in the hills between Chua Tau and Ma Tso Lung villages, and utilise
adjacent lowland, non-grassland habitats for foraging. Ove Arup (2013a) also
reported that the pond of HHW was known to be an important foraging area for
Chinese Pond Herons breeding at the Ho Sheung Heung egretry, although its
significance in this respect appeared to have declined in recent years. Based on the
egretry flight survey results (Ove Arup, 2013b) at Ho Sheng Heung, herons are not

Mammals
A total of 13 mammal species of conservation importance were noted from the
reviewed literature (Ove Arup, 2013a and 2013b; AFCD, 2024). Foremost among
these is Eurasian Otter, which was considered of regional concern by Fellowes et al.
(2002) and was assessed as vulnerable and endangered in China by Wang (1998)
and Jiang et al. (2016), respectively. It is largely restricted to Deep Bay wetlands
where a very small breeding population remains (WWF, 2025). There are several
records of otters at the LMC Meander, the EA, HHW, LMC EEA and OWCAs, as
shown in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.7. Based on the Territory Wide Long-term
Monitoring Survey undertaken by AFCD, Eurasian Otters were observed through
camera trapping between 2011-2014 near the ponds in Liu Pok, as indicated in
60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.7 as Area B (AFCD, unpublished data). In OWCA Area 2,
otters were recorded by camera trap in 2021 (AECOM, 2021) and AFCD in 2024
(AFCD, 2024). Since 2020, Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden (KFBG) have
partnered with WWF-Hong Kong to study otter distribution in Hong Kong, according
to unpublished data by KFBG (2024), 10 otter spraints were found by the research
team at a mitigation pond north of the Project Boundary. McMillan et al. (2022) studied
the population of Eurasian Otter in Hong Kong and suggested that wetland areas
within the HHW were part of their core range, but the exact locations of Eurasian
Otters were not reported. These multiple records extending over a number of years
indicates the HHW area is an existing habitat for Eurasian Otter in Hong Kong.
Eurasian Otter and other mammals (i.e, Small Asian Mongoose (Herpestes
javanicus), Leopard Cat) were also previously recorded from marsh and/or grassland
habitat within the Loop and the EA (Ove Arup, 2013a; AFCD, Unpublished data). The
areas within the Loop have since been developed, and it is expected that these
species would no longer occur in the newly developed habitats.
Herpetofauna
A total of 11 herpetofauna species of conservation importance were reported from
the reviewed literature occurring in the Assessment Area.
A Three-banded Box Turtle was reported by Ove Arup (2013a) to have been recorded
in a hill stream flowing towards Ma Tso Lung during surveys for the NENT NDA PES.
The exact location was not specified in the Report to protect the species from
potential poaching, but it potentially falls outside of the current Assessment Area (the
hilly reaches of the Ma Tso Lung stream fall largely to the south of the Assessment
Area). Ove Arup (2013a) also suggested that streams and riparian areas in Tse Koo
Hang could provide potentially suitable habitat for this species. These habitats do fall
within the Assessment Area, but outside of the Project Boundary. Three-banded Box
Turtle was assessed as critically endangered in the China Red Data Book (Wang and
Zhao, 1998) and has been assessed as a critically endangered species in the IUCN
Red List of Threatened Species in 2018 (IUCN, 2022) and is also a Class II Protected
Animal of China. This species is heavily poached for its unsubstantiated medicinal
value globally, and has therefore been included in Appendix II of CITES and is listed
under the Protection of Endangered Species of Animals and Plants Ordinance (Cap.

586). Furthermore, the Three-banded Box Turtle is listed in Schedule 2 of the Wild
Animals Protection Ordinance (Cap. 170).
Chinese Soft-shelled Turtle (Pelodiscus sinensis) was not found during the ecological
survey stage of the LMC Loop EIA. However, the EIA (Ove Arup, 2013a) notes it has
been reported as widespread in Deep Bay ponds (Karsen et al., 1998). One individual
was seen in a pond at HHW during survey for the Loop and its Peripheral Control
Area Fishponds and Surroundings (Ove Arup, 2013b). Other herpetofauna species
such as Chinese Cobra was also recorded in the EA within the current Project
Boundary (AFCD, Unpublished data).
Butterflies
Previous studies have reported 14 butterfly species of conservation importance from
the Assessment Area, although none were recorded from the current Project
Boundary. These records were made from multiple habitat types, including
concentrations of Grey Scrub Hopper (Aeromachus jhora), Metallic Cerulean
(Jamides alecto) and Small Three-ring (Ypthima norma) from grassy habitats in the
vicinity of Ma Tso Lung Stream.
Odonates
There were nine odonate species of conservation importance from the reviewed
literature, with two species (i.e. Blue Sprite, Ruby Darter) falling within the current
Project Boundary. The habitat associations of many of these records was not reported
from the literature, although some species were noted around ponds (e.g., Sapphire
Flutterer and Scarlet Basker) and Ma Tso Lung Stream (e.g., Blue Chaser
(Potamarcha congener), Ruby Darter).
Aquatic Fauna
Across the reviewed literature, Small Snakehead (Channa asiatica) and the
freshwater crab Somanniathelphusa zanklon were only two aquatic fauna species of
conservation importance with records within the Assessment Area. They were both
recorded at the same watercourse near Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen to the east of the
Project Boundary.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Habitat and Vegetation
Compensatory Wetlands
Ecological Area
The entire EA is approximately 12.78 ha supporting reed marsh and marsh habitats,
6.92 ha of which falls within the Assessment Area. The marsh comprises a mix of
floating, emergent and submerged plants such as Crested Floating Heart
(Nymphoides cristatum), Water Lily (Nymphaea spp.) and Short-leaved Malacca
Galingale (Cyperus malaccensis), while the reedbed is dominated by Common Reed
(Phragmites australis). Specific habitat features to promote usage by Eurasian Otter
had been deployed, including artificial otter holts and otter resting platforms.
OWCA Area 2
Habitat creation works at OWCA Area 2 were completed in October 2022, comprising
6.61 ha pond, 1.66 ha marsh and 0.22 ha reed marsh (CEDD, 2023b). Of these, 4.49
ha fall within the Assessment Area. Specific habitats feature to promote usage by
Eurasian Otter had been provided, including the establishment of otter holts, floating
platforms, and rock platforms. The planting species from open pond bund in Area 2
including Brassica (Brassica oleracea var. alboglabra) and Couch Grass (Cynodon
dactylon). Existing trees, shrubs and dense vegetation were retained, and emergent
plants tolerant of some salinity, such as Short-leaved Malacca Galingale and Mexican
Primrose-willow (Ludwigia octovalvis) were planted.
Pond
A mixture of active, inactive and abandoned aquaculture ponds was dominant across
the HHW Area. Fish-farming devices (e.g., aerators, bird deterrent lines) were
observed in some ponds. While most active ponds do not support submerged or
emergent flora due to the pond profile and management regime, the associated
narrow bunds support disturbance-associated herb and climber species, such as
Couch Grass, Crow-foot Grass (Dactyloctenium aegyptium), Mikania (Mikania
micrantha) and Passion Flower (Passiflora foetida). Fruit trees, such as Mango
(Mangifera indica) and Guava (Psidium guajava), were occasionally cultivated by
villagers on the bunds.
Abandoned ponds were scattered across the HHW Area in the Assessment Area.
These ponds have been colonised by pioneer aquatic herb species in both the interior
and pond bunds, including mono-dominant patches of Blunt Signal-grass (Brachiaria
mutica) and Narrow-leaved Cat-tail (Typha angustifolia). Giant Alocasia (Alocasia
macrorrhiza), White Popinac (Leucaena leucocephala) and Passion Flower were
occasionally encountered. One small pond was recorded near the Ma Tso Lung
Village that appeared to have been abandoned for some time and has become
overgrown with Elephant Grass (Pennisetum purpureum), Knotweed (Polygonum
sp.), and White Popinac. Another pond was recorded located at the junction of border
road and Ma Tso Lung Road, which Winged Cassia (Cassia alata) and other
ornamental species such as Copper Leaf (Acalypha wilkesiana) and Weeping Willow
(Salix babylonica) were recorded at the fringe of pond. One small pond was found
located within a private property at MTL Shun Yee San Tsuen and potentially used
for amenity purpose. Further to the west, two ponds recorded at Hornhill, west to Ping
Hang Stream, appeared to have been abandoned and colonised grassy vegetation,
with Elephant’s Ear (Macaranga tanarius var. tomentosa) and Melastomataceae spp.

recorded on bund. Three small ponds were identified at Tse Koo Hang and between
the Ping Hang to Tai Law Hau area, however the current habitat condition of these
ponds is unclear due to limited access, and potentially used for amenity purpose.
The ECR Alignment would pass through three ponds (Ponds 36-38) to the southeast
to of the LMC Meander. During recent surveys, overgrown vegetation was observed
along bunds and across much of the surface of Ponds 37-38, suggesting they have
been inactive/abandoned for some time. Pond 36 was found to be recently reprofiled,
with the northern portion of the pond partitioned into five smaller units. Another long
abandoned small pond (Pond 39a) that falls partially within the Project Boundary was
found to have been recently reprofiled, changing habitat type from seasonally wet
grassland into a pond, and no vegetation was observed.
Marsh
Marsh areas were recorded as part of the broader HHW wetlands, with Phragmites
vallatorius was very common in the marsh interiors. The edges of the marsh are
colonised by exotic herbs such as Guinea Grass (Panicum maximum) and Narrow-
leaved Cat-tail.
Reed
Two patches of reedbed were identified in HHW, dominated by Phragmites vallatorius
and P. australis. Another patch of reedbed of about 3 ha was identified within the
Loop, dominated by Phragmites spp.
Modified Watercourses
The Ma Tso Lung stream, located west of the Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen,
falls partly within the Construction Area of the Project. Drainage improvement works
undertaken in 2010 resulted in the stream being straightened with highly modified
with concrete banks. Fine sediments were observed deposited in the downstream
section of the channel.
A second modified watercourse occurs in the Assessment Area near the Lo Wu
Range. This watercourse is subject to disturbance, modification and pollution
discharges.
Semi-natural / Natural Watercourse
The LMC Meander is largest natural watercourse recorded in the western portion of
the Assessment Area. Riparian vegetation was dominated by common grass and
herb species such as Giant Alocasia and Gahnia (Gahnia tristis), along with common
tree species including Opposite-leaved Fig (Ficus hispida), Hairy Fig (Ficus hirta),
Common Red-stem Fig (Ficus variegata).
Ping Hang Stream is a small, highly seasonal semi-natural watercourse, originating
from the hillside at Ping Hang, flowing from south to north beneath the Border Road,
through the pond area south of the Loop before discharging into the LMC Meander.
The upper section of the stream course is largely natural, while the lower section has
been straightened and channelised between the surrounding ponds. The lower
section largely retains natural substrates, and bankside vegetation is dominated by
common grassy vegetation such as Para Grass (Brachiaria mutica) and Guinea
Grass.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Another water channel near the upstream of the Ma Tso Lung stream retains a natural
riverbed with gabion channel banks. Aquatic herbaceous species, in particular Ramie
(Boehmeria nivea) and Whorled Pennywort (Hydrocotyle verticillata), formed dense
mats in areas with growing space and appropriate substrate. Several other small
streams originating from Crest Hill, Tit Hang Shan and Ma Tso Lung were recorded
in the Assessment Area. The upstream sections of these watercourses are located
on hillsides and are largely natural and unmodified. Riparian vegetation was observed
along the along these watercourses as previously described.
Seasonally Wet Grassland
An extensive area of seasonally wet grassland was identified south and southwest of
Ma Tso Lung village, with smaller patches found interspersed between pond habitats
in the HHW Area. The seasonally wet grassland was dominated by herb species,
including Freshy Lady-fern (Callipteris esculenta), Taro (Colocasia esculenta),
Morning Glory (Ipomoea cairica), Mikania and Guinea Grass. Scarce individuals of
Lance-leaved Sterculia (Sterculia lanceolata) and White Popinac were also recorded
from this habitat.
Woodland
Woodland belts at Horn Hill bounding the west of Lok Ma Chau Operational Base of
the Hong Kong Police Force and woodland stands near Tse Koo Hang were identified
within the Assessment Area. Native and exotic species were found in this habitat type,
with native plants being more diverse and relatively more abundant. The canopy of
the woodland was dominated by common native tree species and naturally dispersed
fruit tree species in Hong Kong, such as Chinese Hackberry (Celtis sinensis),
Camphor Tree (Cinnamomum camphora) and Longan. The understorey comprised
native tree (e.g. Opposite-leaved Fig, Microcos (Microcos nervosa) and Tetradium
glabrifolium), shrub, climber (e.g. Desmos chinensis) and herb species (e.g. Liriope
spicata). Some exotic plantation species, like Taiwan Acacia and Slash Pine (Pinus
elliottii), were also recorded. Due to the proximity of the woodland habitats to villages,
some agricultural crop species, for instance, Winged Yam (Dioscorea alata), were
found on the edge of the woodland. The at-grade road section of the ECR Alignment
will pass through both recorded woodland areas.
Grassland / Shrubland
Grassland / shrubland within the Assessment Area dominated the hillsides of Crest
Hill, She Leng and Tit Hang Shan, along with unnamed small hills in the southeast.
The grassland / shrubland within the Assessment Area has a simple in floristic
composition, being dominated by Dichotomy Forked Fern (Dicranopteris pedata)
thickets along with common native shrub species Oblong-leaved Litsea (Litsea
rotundifolia var. oblongifolia), Scansorial Climbing Fern (Lygodium scandens),
Common Melastoma (Melastoma malabathricum), Chinese Fevervine (Paederia
scandens) and Rose Myrtle (Rhodomyrtus tomentosa). This habitat is disturbed by
frequent hillfires, with evidence of recent fires observed during the surveys.
Orchard
Scattered orchard patches were recorded at Tse Koo Hang, to the north of Ma Tso
Lung San Tsuen and west of Ma Tso Lung Stream. The orchards were dominated by
Carambola (Averrhoa carambola), Pomelo (Citrus maxima), Wampi (Clausena
lansium), Lychee and Banana (Musa x paradisiaca). The at-grade road section of the

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
ECR Alignment will pass through a small area of orchard to the west of Ma Tso Lung
Stream.
Plantation
Plantations belts / stands were generally found in Ma Tso Lung, near the foot of Crest
Hill and Tit Hang Shan and to the east of Lok Ma Chau Operational Base. Plantation
belts and stands were established for afforestation, amenity, landscaping and
screening purposes, primarily utilising imported pioneer tree species. The plantations
are dominated by exotic trees and fruit trees (e.g. Taiwan Acacia, Cook Pine
(Araucaria columnaris), Brisbane Box (Lophostemon confertus), Lychee and Slash
Pine), interspersed with native pioneer tree species (e.g., Elephant’s Ear, Ivy Tree
(Schefflera heptaphylla), Aporosa (Aporosa dioica), Chinese Banyan (Ficus
macrocarpa) and Camphor Tree). Naturally recruited native small tree and shrub
species, such as Brucea javanica, were likely dispersed from nearby woodlands by
birds. Exotic herbaceous species such as Bidens alba and Mission Grass
(Pennisetum polystachion) were abundant along the edges of these plantation stands.
Agricultural Land
Small patches of agricultural land were observed near villages and scattered in the
Ma Tso Lung area. Food crop (e.g. Lettuce, Lactuca sativa) and fruit tree species (e.g.
Jackfruit, Artocarpus heterophyllus; Longan and Musa acuminata 'Dwarf Cavendish')
were cultivated by villagers in these habitats.
Developed Area
Developed area within the Assessment Area consists of the Loop, roads (e.g. Ma Tso
Lung Road), villages and wasteland (e.g. Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen, Ma
Tso Lung San Tsuen and Ma Tso Lung), government facilities (e.g. Police post, Lok
Ma Chau Operational Base belonging to the Hong Kong Police Force and Hong Kong
Police Lo Wu Range), schools (Lung Kai Public School), and nurseries (King Fung
Nurseries). Areas that are currently being modified or occupied by temporary
structures and construction machinery, or have been previously modified by human
activities but now colonised by exotic vegetation are also classified as Developed
Area. The limited growing space in concrete-paved areas only allows ruderal
herbaceous species and exotic, cultivated landscape, ornamental and fruit tree
species (e.g. Bombax ceiba, Longan, Sterculia monosperma and White Popinac) to
grow in this habitat. The works within the Loop for its development into the Hong
Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park (the Park) commenced in 2018 and
is currently on-going. Amid the COVID-19 epidemic, community isolation and
treatment facilities were constructed on the Loop in early 2022.
Vegetation
A total of 310 plant species were recorded within the Assessment Area during surveys
conducted for this EIA, comprising 192, 113 and 5 are native, exotic and of unknown
origin to Hong Kong respectively (Appendix 8.4 refers). Among the plant species
recorded, 110 were found within the Project Boundary. Plant species and their relative
abundance within each habitat of the Project Boundary and Assessment Area are
listed in Appendix 8.4. Three plant species of conservation importance were
recorded within the Assessment Area, namely Incense Tree, Aralia chinensis and
Tongue Habenaria (Habenaria linguella). Several individuals of Incense Tree were
recorded in the woodland at Tse Koo Hang as well as from a strip of shrubland along

total, four individuals were found within the Construction Area of the Project. Single

shrubland habitat at Tse Koo Hang, outside of the Construction Area of the Project.
Fauna
Avifauna
140 bird species were recorded within the Assessment Area, 81 of which are of
conservation importance. Among the species recorded, 42 were recorded within the
Construction Area of the Project, 15 of which are of conservation importance. Most
of the recorded species are common and widespread in Hong Kong. Details of the
recorded avifauna species recorded in each habitat are presented in Appendix 8.5
and 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.5.
Pond habitats in HHW Area support a high diversity and abundance of waterbirds
and wetland-dependent species, with a total of 105 species and 54 wetland
dependant species recorded from this habitat type. Abundances and diversity were
generally higher in the winter migratory season. Reflecting their generally poor
condition, Ponds 36-38 were found to support a low diversity and abundance of
wetland avifauna, dominated by common species such as White-breasted Waterhen
(Amaurornis phoenicurus), Chinese Pond Heron and Black-crowned Night Heron
(Nycticorax nycticorax). The marsh habitat in HHW area support moderate
abundance and diversity of wetland dependent bird species, including White-
breasted Waterhen and White-throated Kingfisher. Only occasional records of larger
wetland birds (e.g., Grey Heron and Great Egret) were made from this habitat
compared to open water habitat such as pond. Oriental Turtle Dove (Streptopelia
orientalis) was also recorded from the habitat.
Aside from wetland habitats, relatively few records of species of conservation
importance were recorded from other habitats in the Assessment Area. Notably,
Asian Barred Owlet (Glaucidium cuculoides), Chinese Grosbeak (Eophona migratoria)
and Grey Treepie (Dendrocitta formosae) were recorded from woodland habitats, and
several raptor species, including Black Kite, Common Kestrel; Crested Goshawk
(Accipiter trivirgatus); and Eastern Buzzard were recorded flying over various habitats
including grassland / shrubland.
No breeding or nesting activity was recorded during ecological survey, and no records
of Eurasian Eagle Owl or Chinese Francolin (species for which confirmed or
suspected breeding in the Assessment Area was reported in the literature review)
were made. White-throated Kingfisher was recorded from various habitats, including
grassland / shrubland, suggesting it might be breeding in the Assessment Area.
Major Flight Paths
A total of five major flight lines were observed from vantage points adjacent to the
LMC Meander. 12 waterbirds and/or larger avifauna species of conservation
importance, namely Black Kite, Black-crowned Night Heron, Black-faced Spoonbill,
Eastern Cattle Egret, Chinese Pond Heron, Eurasian Spoonbill, Great Cormorant,
Great Egret, Grey Heron, Little Egret, White-throated Kingfisher and Pied Kingfisher
were recorded during the coordinated bird flightline surveys (Table 8.8 refers).

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Mammals
21 mammal species were recorded within the Assessment Area, 16 of which are
considered of conservation importance. Among the species recorded, eight were
recorded within the Construction Area of the Project. The bat species Japanese
Pipistrelle (Pipistrellus abramus) was recorded at various habitats, including wetland
habitats (e.g. pond, compensatory wetland (the EA), marsh, modified watercourse,
semi-natural / natural watercourse and seasonally wet grassland) as well as non-
wetland habitats (e.g. orchard, plantation and developed area). The Short-nosed Fruit
Bat (Cynopterus sphinx) was recorded exclusively in non-wetland habitats. The
Lesser Yellow Bat (Scotophilus kuhlii) was recorded in upper section of the Ma Tso
Lung Stream, and both the Horsfield’s Myotis (Myotis horsfieldii) and Unknown
Vespertilionidae Species 1 were recorded from developed area and modified
watercourse. In addition, Pallas’s Squirrel (Callosciurus erythraeus) was observed
within village / orchard at Ma Tso Lung San Tsuen. Both Small Indian Civet
(Viverricula indica) and Leopard Cat, were captured by camera traps in woodland
habitat. Details of the recorded mammal species recorded in each habitat are
presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.6 and Appendix 8.5B to C. Mammals
species were captured by camera traps were presented in Appendix 8.5A.
While particular attention was given to Eurasian Otter during the ecological surveys
(considering the significance of wetland habitats in HHW to this species), no direct
sightings (during day and night surveys), indirect sightings (from camera traps), or
signs of this species (spraints, footprints) were recorded. Long term and recent
records have shown the presence of Eurasian Otters in the HHW, LMC Meander and
its vicinity as described in Section 8.5.16 and such records have been taken into
account when conducting the impact assessment on the Eurasian Otter.
Herpetofauna
26 herpetofauna species were recorded within the Assessment Area, comprising 11
amphibian and 15 reptile species. Most of the recorded species are widely distributed
throughout Hong Kong, and were predominately observed in orchard and developed
areas. Three of the recorded species are considered of conservation importance:
Chinese Bullfrog, Four-clawed Gecko (Gehyra mutilata), Indian Forest Skink
(Sphenomorphus indicus). Only Chinese Bullfrog and Four-clawed Gecko were
recorded within the Construction Area of the Project, from semi-natural and natural
watercourse and developed area respectively. Details of the recorded herpetofauna
species recorded in each habitat are presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.6 and
Appendix 8.5F to G.
Butterfly
75 butterfly species were recorded within the Assessment Area, most of which are
common and widespread species. A total of 12 recorded species are considered of
conservation importance. Most records of the species of conservation importance
such as Danaid Eggfly Hypolimnas misippus), Pale Palm Dart (Telicota colon),
Peacock Royal (Tajuria cippus), Plain Hedge Blue (Celastrina lavendularis), Small
Three-ring, Swallowtail (Papilio xuthus) and White Royal (Pratapa deva) were from
upland shrubland / grassland habitats. Red-breasted Jezebel (Delias acalis), Metallic
Cerulean and Paintbrush Swift (Baoris farri) were recorded in woodland. Common
Onyx (Horaga onyx) was recorded from seasonally wet grassland, and Grass Demon
(Udaspes folus) was sighted in the low-lying orchard habitat. Three butterfly species
of conservation importance (Metallic Cerulean, Red-breast Jezebel and Paintbrush

Odonate
32 odonate species were recorded within the Assessment Area, including five
odonate species of conservation importance: Blue Chaser, Coastal Glider
(Macrodiplax cora), Dingy Dusk-hawker (Gynacantha subinterrupta), Sapphire
Flutterer and Scarlet Basker. Most of the recorded odonate species are
common/abundant and widespread in Hong Kong. Eight odonate species were
recorded within the Construction Area of the Project, none of which are considered
species of conservation importance. Details of the recorded odonate species
recorded in each habitat are presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.6 and Appendix
8.5J to K.
Firefly
Three firefly species were recorded within the Assessment Area, one of which,
Motschulsky’s Starworm (Rhagophthalmus motschulskyi), is considered of
conservation importance. Motschulsky’s starworm was recorded from seasonally wet
grassland in the Ma Tso Lung area. While this species is currently considered
endemic to Hong Kong, it is much more commonly encountered in villages and
farmlands, even in urban parks, than in wild places. (Yiu, 2023). No firefly species of
conservation importance were recorded within the Construction Area of the Project.
Details of the recorded firefly species recorded in each habitat are presented in
60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.6 and Appendix 8.5L to M.
Freshwater Communities
24 freshwater aquatic faunal species were recorded within the Assessment Area,
including the freshwater crab Somanniathelphusa zanklon and the fish Gobiopterus
macrolepis, which are both species of conservation importance. Three individuals of
Somanniathelphusa zanklon were recorded in the upstream of Ping Hang Stream.
Two individuals of Gobiopterus macrolepis were recorded in the riparian zone of the
LMC Meander. Notably, one individual of freshwater fish Blotched Snakehead
(Channa maculata), classified as high risk of extinction in Hong Kong by the WWF
HK State of Hong Kong Biodiversity report (WWF, 2025), was recorded at modified
watercourse outside of the Project Boundary. The recorded individual is likely to be
escaped cultivated individual from nearby ponds based on the location of discovery.
No species of conservation importance were recorded within the Construction Area
of the Project. Details of the recorded freshwater fauna species recorded in each
habitat are presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.6 and Appendix 8.5N to O.
Evaluation of Ecological Value
The ecological importance of habitats within the Assessment Area was evaluated with
reference to the criteria stipulated in Annex 8 of EIAO-TM, as summarised in Table

Overall ecological value
The overall ecological valuation of habitats recorded in the Assessment Area under
this Study is generally consistent with that from the LMC Loop EIA, with ponds in
HHW remaining of high ecological value; reedbeds of moderate ecological value;
modified watercourses of low to moderate ecological value; semi-natural and natural
watercourses ranging from low to moderate, moderate to high and high ecological
value depending on locations, seasonally wet grassland and grassland and shrubland
habitats in the Ma Tso Lung area of low to moderate ecological value, orchard,
agricultural land and developed areas retaining ecological values from very low to
low.
Notable differences between the two assessments reflect changes in site conditions,
the establishment of new ecological features, and the fact that habitat assessments
under the LMC Loop EIA covered a larger geographic area including other habitat
patches. The EA and OWCAs, which were not established during preparation of the
LMC Loop EIA, are newly assessed as having moderate to high ecological value.
Reedbed in the HHW is reassessed as moderate ecological value as it is only
seasonally wet and supports moderate fauna species richness. Scattered ponds
recorded within the Assessment Area, which were not individually assessed in the
LMC Loop EIA, are considered of low ecological value under this study. Woodland
habitats, formerly rated as low to moderate ecological value, are reassessed as being
of moderate ecological value given that they were found to support moderate faunal
species richness and to have connectivity to nearby natural habitats. Plantation
habitats, formerly rated low to moderate ecological value, are considered as low
ecological value due to their fragmented distribution and limited plant diversity.
Species of Conservation Importance
With reference to Annex 8 of EIAO-TM, the ecological value of species recorded
within the Assessment Area was assessed in Table 8.22, in terms of protection /
conservation status (e.g. fauna protected under local legislation (except birds)),
status under regional / global legislation / conventions, species distribution (e.g.
endemic), and rarity (e.g. rare or restricted).

Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Identification of Potential Environmental Impacts
Construction Phase – Direct Impacts
Direct Impact on Recognised Sites of Conservation Importance and other
Ecologically Sensitive Receivers
Within the Assessment Area, five recognised sites of conservation importance
(proposed HHW WCP, WCA, WBA, “CA” zone and Priority Site for Enhanced
Conservation), and other ecologically sensitive receivers including IBA, the EA and
OWCA Area 2, off-site compensation woodland, and key dragonfly site in Ma Tso
Lung) were identified. Part of the Assessment Area is also recognised as an Important
Bird Area (IBA) and regarded as an ecologically sensitive resource under this project.
The potentially affected recognised sites of conservation importance and other
ecologically sensitive receivers are located in the HHW area as well as area to the
southeast of the Loop.
A total of 13 habitats were identified within the Assessment Area, including both
wetland and non-wetland habitats (Section 8.6 refers). The Construction Area of the
Project will encroach on all identified habitat types except reedbed and agricultural
land. The potentially affected wetland habitats are mainly in the EA and WCA to the
southeast of the Loop.
The ECR Alignment has been shifted northward to minimise the slope works in Tse
Koo Hang, which would lead to an unavoidable encroachment into the area within the
proposed HHW WCP as indicated in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.1. Nevertheless, the
encroachment is located at the fringe of the proposed HHW WCP boundary. The ECR
layout is expected to be finalised prior to the detailed studies for the HHW WCP,
therefore potential interface issues will be further reviewed and addressed at the
detailed studies stage as indicated in the WCPs System FS (AFCD, 2024a).
Areas inside the Construction Area of the Project would be affected by construction
works, resulting in direct impacts on wetland habitats within the sites of conservation
importance and other ecological sensitive receivers, mainly within the WCA, WBA,
“CA” zone, Priority Site for Enhanced Conservation, the EA, as well as the IBA. The
portion of the EA included in the Project Boundary but outside the 0.38ha
Construction area of the Project would not be affected or occupied as temporary
works/storage areas. To avoid construction activities and to deter other unwanted
human access, such area would be properly fenced off and maintained by the project
proponent during the construction phase. Fences to be installed during the
construction phase will incorporate a 30cm gap at the bottom to allow passage of
otters and other mammal, reducing the potential impacts of wildlife on accessing the
EA, subject to the Contractor’s design. Although the boundary of Key Dragonfly Site
in Ma Tso Lung has not been delineated, it generally refers to the mosaic of
freshwater ponds, abandoned ponds and abandoned paddies lying in the former
Frontier Closed Area to the east of Lok Ma Chau. For conservative assessment
purposes, this ecological sensitive resource is considered to be directly impacted by
the Construction Area of the Project. Considering the importance of these sites
affected, the loss of these wetlands would be considered of moderate to high
significance, in the absence of mitigation measures. The woodland habitat within the
aforementioned areas is connected to natural habitats nearby (e.g. hillside grassland)
supporting moderately diverse and abundant flora and fauna communities. As such,
the loss of this habitat is considered to be of moderate significance. Relatively low

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Direct Impacts to Habitat and Vegetation
Overview of Direct Impact to Habitats
Considerable thought went into selecting the most appropriate ECR alignment and
design from environmental and engineering perspectives, with a detailed option
review process considered the base scheme and preferred location (see Section 2.5
for details). In summary, the ECR will comprise a single 4-lane two-way carriage way,
variously in the form of at-grade road, depressed road, underpass and viaduct, of a
total length of approximately 2.5km. The preferred ECR Alignment avoids and
minimises impacts to the Recognised Sites of Conservation Importance / Other
Ecologically Sensitive Receivers and wetland habitats as far as practicable, with the
section (of about 1.2 km long) that will traverse the EA, LMC Meander and three
Ponds 36-38 being constructed as a shallow underpass (approximately 12m below
ground). In order to minimise the extent of excavation so as to conserve adjacent
wetland habitats, excavation and lateral support of this section would be used for the
“cut and cover” construction of the underpass below ground as detailed Section 2.6.
The ECR Alignment then follows the course of the existing Border Road northwest
either as a viaduct or at-grade, before looping to the south and extending to the
planned KTN NDA behind (to the east of) Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen. The
LMC Meander, marsh and Ponds 36-38 included in the Project Boundary but outside
of Construction Area of the Project would not be fenced off (except the EA as
discussed in S.8.8.4) and would not be occupied as temporary works/ storage area.
In addition, Ponds 36-38 would be maintained by the project proponent during the
construction phase (S. 8.11.18 refers)
A fully enclosed electrical mechanical plant room (hereinafter referred to as E&M
plant room) and drainage pumping room will be provided to support the operation of
the depressed road and underpass. The dimensions and size of the proposed E&M
plan room and drainage pumping room will be determined during the detailed design
stage. The indicative location of the proposed E&M plant room and drainage pumping
room is presented in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.10. For conservative impact
estimation, habitats across the entire potential area where these facilities will be
located are assumed to be directly and permanently lost.
Development of the Project will result in temporary and permanent direct loss of
habitats and vegetation within the Construction Area of the Project. Permanent
habitat loss will result from construction works, whereby the habitat will be developed
and no longer available for wildlife use, while temporary habitat loss under the Project
will mainly arise from habitats that fall within the Construction Area, but will be
reinstated / revitalised once the construction works are completed. The identified
habitats losses are summarised in Table 8.24.

Direct Impacts to Compensatory Wetlands
The EA along the southeastern edge of the Loop has been established since
December 2022. It is considered of moderate to high ecological value, with species
of conservation importance including Little Egret, Grey Heron, and Pied Kingfisher
recorded during recent surveys (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.5 refers). The ECR
Alignment will traverse the EA as an underpass. Cut and cover construction will result
in the temporary loss of 0.38 ha of the EA, which would be reinstated following the
completion of construction works. The areas of the EA adjacent to 0.38 ha the works
areas will be fenced off and maintained as wetland habitat during the construction
phase, and not used for temporary access, works/storage area and other
construction-related activities. Details of construction works near / in the EA (including
but not limited to working schedule/period, construction method, reinstatement
method, use of equipment, type and route of vehicle entry and water supply
arrangements) will be carefully considered and incorporated during the detailed
design stage to minimise impacts to the EA. Given that the EA was established as a
compensatory wetland, according to the ongoing monitoring data the EA after its
establishment, it supports moderate flora and moderate to high fauna diversity,
temporary ecological impacts would be considered to be moderate to high in scale,
in the absence of mitigation measures.
Direct Impacts to Ponds
The ECR Alignment would traverse pond habitats to the south of the Loop as an
underpass. The construction of shallow underpass would primarily cause temporary
loss of habitat at three ponds (Ponds 36 to 38). As discussed in Sections 8.6.6, the
condition of these ponds is relatively poor, although there are some records of
wetland species or species of conservation importance were recorded during recent
surveys or from other available data (i.e., HKBWS, 2018-2023; AFCD, 2024b). It is
also recognised that these ponds form part of the larger wetland system in LMC/HHW
area and have significant potential for restoration.
The affected pond habitats would total 1.51 ha during construction phase. Despite
poor condition of the ponds, and considering their ecological function as part of the
larger wetland system of HHW, temporary direct ecological impacts to these habitats
would be moderate to high in scale, in the absence of mitigation measures. As the
affected ponds will largely be reinstated and enhanced after the construction works
are completed (detailed below in Section 8.11.14), permanent operation phase
impacts are considered minor in scale.
Direct Impacts to Marsh
Construction Area of the Project will result in the permanent loss of 0.23 ha of
freshwater marsh along the Border Road and temporary loss of 0.10 ha of freshwater
marsh immediately to the south of the LMC Meander. Marsh habitat is considered of
moderate ecological value, with species of conservation significance recorded from
the habitat including Japanese Pipistrelle and wetland-dependent species such as
White-breasted Waterhen and White-throated Kingfisher. Considering the existing
quality and associated common species of this habitat, the loss of this habitat is
therefore considered to be moderate in scale.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Direct Impacts to Modified Watercourse
The ECR Alignment would avoid direct impacts to the lower sections of Ma Tso Lung
Stream, crossing the stream as a viaduct. The viaduct piers would be located outside
of the watercourse and its riparian zone, and no construction activities would be
conducted within the watercourse or riparian zone. The affected section of the
watercourse does not support high densities of disturbance-sensitive species and
given that the viaduct section of the ECR Alignment would be elevated approximately
20m above the affected watercourses, the riparian vegetation along or adjacent to
the watercourse would not be significantly affected by the shadow effect of the viaduct.
Hence, no loss of this habitat is anticipated.
Direct Impacts to Semi-natural / Natural Watercourse
LMC Meander
The ECR Alignment will traverse the LMC Meander as an underpass, avoiding
permanent impacts. However, cut and cover construction will result in temporary loss
of the water channel and associated riparian vegetation, totalling approximately
0.21ha (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.9 refers). The LMC Meander is considered of high
ecological value and was found to support species of conservation importance such
as Eurasian Otter and Chinese Bullfrog, as well being utilised as a flight path by
avifauna species including Black-faced Spoonbill, Great Egret, Great Cormorant.
These temporary ecological impacts would be considered to be moderate to high in
scale, in the absence of mitigation measures.
Ping Hang Stream and Other Watercourses
The ECR Alignment will avoid permanent direct impacts to Ping Hang stream.
However, cut and cover construction will require that the Stream (approximately
0.4km) is temporarily diverted. The diversion works in themselves are considered a
relatively low scale impact, as the diverted channel would be similar to the existing
semi-natural stream that runs through the pond area. Ecological impacts would be
considered to be minor in the absence of mitigation measures. Aside from Ping Hang
Stream, a small section of watercourse (0.02 ha) located to the east of Ma Tso Lung
Village will also fall within the Construction Area of the Project. However, the ECR
Alignment would cross this stream as a viaduct, no construction activities would
therefore be conducted within the watercourse or its riparian zone, with no
encroachment on the watercourse and its riparian zone by the viaduct piers. The
affected section of the watercourse does not support high densities of disturbance-
sensitive species, and given that the viaduct section of the ECR Alignment would be
elevated approximately 25m above the affected watercourses, the riparian vegetation
along or adjacent to the watercourse would not be significantly affected by the
shadow effect of the viaduct. Hence, no loss of this habitat is anticipated
Direct Impacts to Seasonally Wet Grassland Habitats
Several patches of seasonally wet grassland totalling 1.61 ha would be permanently
lost under the Project. The habitat was found to support only low flora and fauna
diversity, with an overall low-to-moderate ecological value. Given its ecological value
and small size, the impact on the loss of this habitat is considered to be low to
moderate in scale only.

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Direct Impacts to Woodland Habitat
The ECR Alignment will pass through the woodland habitats alongside the existing
Border Road. A total of 1.68 ha of woodland would be permanently lost. It is expected
some associated flora species of conservation importance (e.g. Incense Tree) within
the affected woodlands would also be directly impacted by the project construction.
The significance of this impact to woodland is considered to moderate in scale, given
the moderately diverse and abundant flora and fauna communities supported by
woodland habitats, and the ecological linkage of woodlands with large areas of
adjacent natural habitats (e.g. hillside grassland).
Direct Impacts to Other Habitats
Approximately 2.88 ha grassland / shrubland would be permanently lost due to
development of the Project. The affected low-lying grasslands were found to
supported limited diversity and abundance of wildlife, and impacted by disturbance
from nearby by human activities, therefore the direct impact on this habitat is
considered of low scale if no mitigation measures are adopted. Other habitats directly
impacted by the Project (Orchard, Plantation) are of low ecological value with
relatively small areas affected. Considering the low ecological value and low wildlife
diversity and abundance supported, the loss of these habitats is considered a
negligible to minor ecological impact. 5.15ha of existing Developed Area would be
directly impacted by the project, and there would be no direct habitat loss of reedbed,
modified watercourse or agricultural land habitats.
Habitat Fragmentation
Fragmentation refers to a discontinuity in habitat, decreasing its carrying capacity,
hindering movement, and rendering it less attractive to flora and fauna (Haddad et al.,
2015), or the isolation of individuals of a species’ population resulting in their lower
viability (Schlaepfer et al., 2018). The ECR Alignment will pass through lower value
habitats (including developed area, small patches of grassland/shrubland and
plantation) adjacent to Ma Tso Lung Shun Yee San Tsuen and Ma Tso Lung San
Tsuen mainly on a viaduct, therefore habitat fragmentation impacts in these areas
are anticipated to be minor. Fragmentation is anticipated to be more significant where
the ECR Alignment passes through/adjacent to wetland and woodland habitats.
Fragmentation of Wetlands and Associated Fauna
Habitat fragmentation is expected to occur where the ECR Alignment crosses pond
habitats, the EA and LMC Meander. This is of concern as the affected habitats
supports major flight paths between the wetland habitats in the LMC/HHW area (on
the east) and the San Tin area (on the west). As such, it is of importance particularly
for Eurasian Otters which potentially use the area to transit between HHW and ST /
SPS, as well as large wetland avifaunal species, which use the corridor as a flight
path. These fragmentation impacts would be mostly temporary in nature, restricted to
the construction phase, as the ECR will cross the area as a shallow underpass, with
only two reinforced concrete ventilation openings (each approximately 0.13ha)
remaining at grade following the completion of works. Nevertheless, the scale of
these impacts during the construction phase are anticipated to be moderate if no
mitigation measures are implemented.
Other potential wetland fragmentation impacts are expected to be lower in scale. The
seasonally wet grassland habitat to the north of Tse Koo Hang is already fragmented

Direct Impact on Species of Conservation Importance and Associated Habitats
Flora
Only one flora species of conservation importance, Incense Tree, was recorded within
the Construction Area of the Project during previous and current surveys. Four
individual incense trees were recorded in the developed area and woodland habitat
to the north of Tse Koo Hang during recent surveys, inside the Construction Area of

are regarded as a minor to moderate in significance if no mitigation measures are

8.11.29.
Avifauna
A total of 15 avifauna species of conservation importance were recorded within the
Construction Area of the Project during recent surveys. The majority of these species
were wetland-dependent species recorded from ponds, with some species recorded
from other wetland habitats (i.e. seasonally wet grassland, modified watercourse,
semi-natural / natural watercourse and marsh) and non-wetland habitat (i.e.
woodland). Considering the high mobility of avifauna species, it is anticipated that
these species would be displaced and utilise nearby similar habitats during
construction, therefore no major direct injury/mortality impacts are anticipated.
Considering the general low avifauna usage at all habitats within the Construction
Area of the Project but high ecological linkage to adjacent wetland habitats, the
impact of loss of foraging ground is considered a minor to moderate impact with no
mitigation in place.
Breeding adult avifauna, chicks and eggs are more vulnerable to construction works
and higher risk of direct injury / mortality. Although no breeding activities were
observed during the current survey, precautionary measures such as pre-
construction survey should be carried out within and adjacent to the Construction
Area of the Project, as well as proposed enhancement areas, to avoid any potential
direct injuries to breeding pairs, chicks or eggs of avifauna species of conservation
importance.

Direct Injury / Mortality on Other Wildlife
Aside from the species described in the previous sections, construction activities may

Bird Collision
Construction activities may cause potential injury / mortality impacts to birds in flight,
particularly for waterbirds using the HHW Flight Corridor and other flight paths along
the EA and HHW area. Construction structures, heavy machinery (e.g. cranes),
materials that are difficult to see (e.g. cables, wires) and night-time lighting would be
of particular concern. Records of birds using the major flight corridors were generally
15 - 25m above ground level or higher (Sections 8.5.14, 8.6.27 to 8.6.29 refers). No
construction activities would be undertaken at 15m above existing ground level or
higher along the flightpaths, so general construction activities (as presented in
Appendix 2.1) are unlikely to pose a significant mortality/injury risk to avifauna.
Nevertheless, a small proportion of birds (less than 5% usage ) were recorded flying
below 15m near LMC Meander and the EA according to the EM&A programme under
the LMC Loop EIA (CEDD, 2023a). Therefore, the potential impact is considered of
minor to moderate in significance only.
The majority of ardeids utilising the seasonal active night roost near Ma Tso Lung
Road as illustrated in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.8 were observed flying northwards
to ponds in the HHW Area, and therefore no significant collision risks are expected
