Disturbance and Obstruction of Flight Path
Construction activities and tall machinery could potentially obstruct/disrupt the major
flight paths in the area to the east of the Loop, including the HHW Flight Corridor.
Movement of waterbirds between their roosting / breeding sites and foraging grounds
could be hindered if the birds adopt a higher flight path, or adjust the flight path
alignment, to avoid disturbance from construction activities. This would result in
increased energy expenditure and reduced foraging efficiency. This potential
disturbance impact is anticipated to be moderate without mitigation. Mitigation
measures such as scheduling construction activities to avoid simultaneous works
within sensitive wetland areas (i.e. Zone 1, Zone 2 and Zone 3 as illustrated in

implemented as far as practicable to minimise this impact.

The seasonally active night roost recorded from plantation habitat at the northern end

adjacent to Ma Tso Lung Road, suggesting some degree of disturbance tolerance,
therefore the potential disturbance impact is anticipated to minor in significance. The

nearby habitats and result in the displacement of fauna. Construction activities carried
out at or above existing ground level (such as silent piling by press-in method,
cofferdam construction, movement/using of construction machinery) will be visible
and audible from the surrounding environment and therefore more likely to disturb
waterbirds and other wetland-dependent species, particularly sensitive habitats in the
EA, LMC Meander and Ponds 36 - 38 adjacent to the Construction Area of the Project
as illustrated in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.9. Underground construction of the
depressed road and underpass, which will be undertaken using a cut-and-cover
method, will occur largely below ground once construction of cofferdams is completed
and the excavation has reached the final depth, with all designed struts and supports
installed. Excavation, strut installation, and structural works will be undertaken within
fully enclosed conditions, which significantly reducing the potential disturbance to
nearby wetlands and wildlife. Moreover, the noise disturbance would be managed
through established noise and vibration control measures, including use of QPME
and moveable noise barriers/enclosures.
Extent of Disturbance Impacts
During construction of the Project, disturbance to surrounding habitats is anticipated
mainly in the form of noise from silent piling by press-in method, excavation and
machinery, as well as visual disturbance. Such activities are expected to influence
the use of adjacent habitats by disturbance-sensitive fauna, particularly large
waterbirds and mammals.
The severity of impacts will vary across species groups. Large waterbirds such as
herons, egrets and cormorants are considered particularly sensitive and are likely to
avoid disturbed areas (Yang et al, 2021; Ove, 2013a). Long term monitoring data of
waterbirds from Mai Po Inner Deep Bay Ramsar Site Waterbird Monitoring
Programme submitted by HKBWS to AFCD and EIA field survey results were
reviewed; records indicate that several large water bird species have been observed
using Ponds 36-41 (60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.2). The ECR Alignment would traverse
Ponds 36-38 directly, while Ponds 39-41 would fall within the disturbance zone
associated with the Construction Area of the Project.
Considering there are a number of disturbance sensitive species recorded from
habitats in the vicinity of the Construction Area of the Project, a quantitative estimate
of the potential extent of disturbance impacts has been developed adopting the
following criteria:
• Exclusion Zone (EZ): Close to the source, disturbance levels are high enough
to prevent disturbance sensitive species from using habitats in the zone, even
if they would provide suitable habitat for the species in the absence of
disturbance.
• Reduced Density Zone (RDZ): Further from the source, disturbance sensitive
species would use suitable habitats but likely at a reduced density compared to
undisturbed habitats. In this zone, it is assumed 0% usage of the habitat closest
to the disturbance source, and 100% usage furthest from the source. Overall,
usage in the reduced density zone is therefore considered to be 50% of that in
undisturbed habitats.
Previous EIA reports in the NWNT including the LMC Loop EIA (AEIAR-176/2013),
LMC Spur Line EIA (AEIAR-052/2002) and STLMC DN EIA (AEIAR-261/2024) have
adopted similar approaches in assessing disturbance impacts, assuming EZ and

2013a; CEDD & PlanD, 2024). Calculating the EZs and RDZs for larger, and
commonly occurring disturbance sensitive waterbirds species (such as Great
Cormorant, Great Egret, Grey Heron and Black-faced Spoonbill) will effectively
delineate the maximum extent of ecological disturbance resulting from the Project (i.e.
it can be assumed that indirect impacts to other less disturbance sensitive species
would not extend beyond these zones). Raptor species such as Greater Spotted
Eagle, Imperial Eagle, Osprey and Crested Serpent Eagle were also recorded
occurring within the Assessment Area from literature review and recent surveys.
While these species are considered very sensitive to disturbance, the abundance of
these raptors in the Assessment Area is extremely low (varying from 0 to 3 from
recent surveys). Moreover, records of these species are often closely associated
with prey availability rather than habitat area per se. For example, monitoring data
from the LMC EEA has indicated presence of multiple Imperial and Greater Spotted
Eagles within a relatively small area of enhanced wetland (MTR, 2024), indicating
that prey availability is a key driver for the distribution and abundance of these species.
Therefore, adopting these raptor species (that occur in very low abundance and often
distributed according to prey availability) as indicators for calculating EZs and RDZs
is not representative of disturbance impacts to wetland communities more broadly.
The extent of EZ and RDZ adopted in previous EIA’s differs from Project to Project.
For example, the San Tin Technopole EIA (CEDD & PlanD, 2024) adopts various
zoning distances, up to a 0-200m EZ and 200-400m RDZ in relation to the
construction of high-rise buildings. This reflects the extensive disturbance expected
from high-rise construction works, as well as the very large scale of the Project and
high value of the affected wetlands. In contrast, the Loop adopts an EZ of 0-50m and
a RDZ of 50-100m for at-grade roads. These zones were considered suitable given
the lower overall disturbance expected from at-grade works. For the current project,
an EZ of 0-50m and a RDZ of 50-100m will also be adopted for wetland habitats
potentially supporting disturbance sensitive species. This is considered appropriate
given that the majority of the ECR alignment running through/adjacent to wetland
habitats will be either at-grade or underground. Indeed, this approach to disturbance
zoning is considered conservative given that construction activities within the wetland
areas would primarily occur below existing ground level, and most of the working
areas would be covered within excavation cofferdam during the construction phase
as described in Section 8.8.41. Therefore, the potential disturbance to avifauna from
construction (i.e. noise, vibration, lighting and human presence) is expected to be
lower than that associated with typical surface construction works. The use of
hoarding, quieter piling methods (e.g. silent piling by press-in method), restrictions on
tall plant machinery, and non-percussive construction methods will further reduce the
disturbance magnitude. As also noted in the LMC Loop EIA, animals and birds
generally habituate more readily to constant, non-explosive noise and are less
affected by non-visual forms of disturbance.
The proposed ECR Alignment comprises depressed road, underpass, at-grade
carriageway, and viaduct sections, connecting the Loop and the Kwu Tung North New

of the viaduct section at Ma Tso Lung is considered comparable to that of the at-
grade section, as:
• The adjacent habitats that support potentially disturbance sensitive species (e.g.
Pond 93) are already subject to disturbance from existing human activities and
traffic volume. According to long-term monitoring data from the HKBWS and

are anticipated to be minor in significance.
Disturbance to Watercourse Habitat (LMC Meander)
Disturbance impacts to the LMC Meander are anticipated to be of moderate to high
significance considering the LMC meander had previous records of Eurasian Otter,
and it is also an ecological corridor for waterbirds and mammals.
Disturbance to Other Wetland Habitats
Apart from the LMC Meander, the remaining watercourses in the Assessment Area
are relatively small and are subject to some level of disturbance already, whereas the
section of Ma Tso Lung Stream within the Construction Area of the Project is
channelised and located in a disturbed area. Only very low occurrence of disturbance
sensitive species was observed from these habitats during recent surveys. Given that
the viaduct section of the ECR Alignment would be elevated approximately 20m
above the affected watercourses, the riparian vegetation along or adjacent to the
watercourse would not be significantly affected by the shadow effect of the viaduct.
Therefore, the potential disturbance impact is considered to be insignificant.

Other wetland habitats including marsh and seasonally wet grassland in the HHW
area are located along the Construction Area of the Project and would also be subject
to construction disturbance. The affected marsh and seasonally wet grassland areas
support a relatively low diversity of species, which are generally tolerant to
disturbance (CEDD & PlanD, 2024) with wetland avifauna recorded during recent
surveys typically being less disturbance sensitive species such as White-breasted
Waterhen and White-throated Kingfisher. Only a few records of other large,
disturbance sensitive species (e.g. Grey Heron and Great Egret) were made from
these affected habitats compared to open water habitat such as pond. According to
long-term avifaunal monitoring results of EM&A programme for the WCR (CEDD,
2023a), Pond 12 indicated in 60722948/A10/FIGURE 8.8 has changed from pond to
marsh as observed before commencement of the WCR works. Under the updated
habitat condition, the avifaunal assemblage recorded from 62 survey events from
March 2022 to August 2023 indicates that the pond is now supports reed marsh-
dependent species (e.g. Yellow Bittern, White-breasted Waterhen), along with other
common and widespread terrestrial species. No significant impact on the bird usage
of Pond 12 was observed arising from the WCR construction activities and its
proximity based on EM&A monitoring data. The avifaunal species recorded within the
marsh and seasonally wet grassland habitat from the ecological surveys of the ECR
Project are consistent with the species composition observed in Pond 12. Therefore,
disturbance impacts on seasonally wet grassland and marsh are considered to be of
low significance.
Disturbance to Other Non-Wetland Habitats
Non-wetland habitats recorded in the vicinity of the Construction Area of the Project,
mostly comprise shrubland / grassland, plantation and woodland. These habitats are
located on both sides of the existing Border Road, with a large patch of woodland
habitat located to the north of Tse Koo Hang. Although these habitats are generally
of low or low to moderate ecological value (apart from the moderate ecological value
woodland), several individuals of Incense Trees, and some mammal and butterfly
species of conservation importance were recorded in the woodland habitat to the
north of Tse Koo Hang. Dust and pollutants generated during construction phase
could deposit on leaves and affect growth of vegetation, in turn degrading the habitats.
Construction activities would also bring disturbance to these habitats and associated
wildlife. However, given these habitats are already subject to disturbance from traffic
and other human activities, and that the fauna species recorded are generally mobile
and recorded in other areas further from the ECR Alignment. The woodland
peripheries are expected to function as natural buffers that help shield the core
woodland areas from construction-related disturbance. Good site practices and
standard mitigation measures, including the erection of hoardings around active
works areas, will be implemented to further reduce disturbance to adjacent non-
wetland habitats. Therefore, the potential construction disturbance impact to non-
wetland habitats is anticipated to be of minor significance.
Breeding and nesting birds may be more sensitive to disturbance than at other times.
Eurasian Eagle Owl is known to occur in the grassland/shrubland habitats in the hilly
areas between HHW and Tse Koo Hang, and potentially breeds in these habitats.
However, overseas studies indicate the home range of this species is very large, up
to 25km2 (Kang C et al, 2013), therefore potential disturbance impacts are considered
to be of low significance as affected habitats are likely to form only a very small fringe
of the species total range. Chinese Francolin and White-throated Kingfisher have also
been observed exhibited breeding or nesting behaviours within the hillside grassland

Night-time Disturbance
Uncontrolled night-time lighting and glare from the construction sites has the potential
to impact the light-sensitive cycles of roosting avifauna and activity of nocturnal fauna
(e.g. Eurasian Otters, bats, herpetofauna and firefly) in the vicinity, potentially
affecting migration, foraging and breeding success of these species. Overall, these
species are already subject to minor nocturnal disturbance from nearby traffic and
human activities at the nearby the Loop, intense artificial lights from construction sites
would pose greater disturbance to these species and associated habitats, which is of
moderate impact if unmitigated. Appropriate measures would be adopted to minimise
night-time glare impacts.
Firefly species Motschulsky’s Starworm, which was recorded at seasonally wet
grassland close to Ma Tso Lung Village, breeding behaviour may potentially be
impacted by the glare generated from the Construction Area of the Project along the
hillside. Considering that there is a considerable distance (120 m) from the
Construction Area of the Project, and that the species is more commonly encountered
in disturbed areas such as village (or even in urban parks) compared to the wild (Yiu,
2023), it suggested that the species is tolerant to some level of disturbance and night-
time lighting. It is therefore considered to have minor significance of indirect impacts
on this species of conservation importance from glare/lighting generated from the
Project.

waterbodies. Sediment particles may cause physical injury to aquatic fauna and
potentially clog the respiratory systems of fish and invertebrates. In addition, the
potential discharge of pollutants or chemicals could lead to bioaccumulation and
biomagnification within the Deep Bay ecosystem, thereby posing risks to waterbirds
and other aquatic communities. Potential impacts on water quality are considered
moderate in significance if unmitigated.
Prior to the commencement of works, all water in ponds and wetland areas inside the
Construction Area of the Project Construction would need to be drained. This drained
water could contain sediments and/or other pollutants (i.e., nutrients), so direct
discharge of these drained waters to nearby watercourses will therefore be prohibited.
The drained waters will be temporarily stored for on-site reuse as far as practicable,

rainfall and water pumped from LMC Meander during construction phase of the ECR

Contractor will use portable pumps to provide supplemental water supply from LMC
Meander to maintain adequate water levels in the remaining parts of the EA, thereby
sustaining the reedbed and freshwater marsh habitats. In case of non-compliance of
water quality within the EA specified in Table 8.1 of CEDD (2022), appropriate water
pollution control measures (e.g., emergency bypass mechanism) shall be carried out
by the contractor to prevent polluted water entering the EA. Before pumping the water
from LMC Meander to the EA, the Contractor will test water quality of LMC Meander,

Operation phase wetland habitat fragmentation impacts have largely been addressed
through the Project design: where the ECR Alignment passes through the sensitive

Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
Cumulative Ecological Impacts
The construction works of the Project will tentatively commence in Q1 / Q2 2027, and
completed by Q4 2031. A full list of concurrent projects is detailed in Chapter 2. The
cumulative impact assessment for ecology covers the vicinity of Hoo Hok Wai and
Ma Tso Lung, where the Assessment Area would overlap with several major
development projects which would be at various stages of construction/operation.
Potential cumulative impacts may arise from the combined effect of concurrent
projects within the Assessment Area with potential ecological impacts, including:-
• Development of the Loop
• Development of the proposed Hoo Hok Wai Wetland Conservation Park under
the Wetland Conservation Park System
• Ma Tso Lung Area and Other Sites in Kwu Tung North New Development Area
and North District – Feasibility Study
• Northern Metropolis Highway (San Tin to Kwu Tung Section)
Cumulative Impacts on Wetland Habitats and Sites of Conservation Importance
Impacts to wetland habitats arising from the Development of the Loop (excluding ECR
Development) includes habitat loss within the Loop, along the “Direct Link” (from the
Loop to the LMC station), and along the WCR (along Ha Wan Tsuen Road East).
Additional disturbance impacts were predicted in areas of wetland alongside
construction works. The areas of directly and indirectly impacted wetlands affected
by development within the Loop are partially included in the current Assessment Area,
while wetlands affected by the proposed “Direct Link” and WCR are not within the
current Project Assessment Area. Construction of buildings within the Loop
commenced in 2024 and is expected to be fully completed by 2035, overlapping with
the construction period of the current Project. However, cumulative impacts to
wetlands and consequent effects on fauna species of conservation importance is
anticipated to be low, as mitigation measures required under the LMC Loop EIA
(including establishment of the EA and OWCAs) have already been implemented.
Temporary impacts to a small portion of the EA resulting from development of the
ECR Project would be mitigated by the provision and maintenance of compensatory
wetlands in the OWCAs as described in Section 8.11 of this report. The affected EA
would be reinstated to the satisfaction of the future maintenance agent in accordance
with a reinstatement and monitoring plan during the construction phase (Section
8.8.8 refers). The footprint of the ECR alignment is not anticipated to result in adverse
ecological impacts on wetland habitats upon completion by Q4 2031 as described in
Section 8.8.67. Cumulative impacts on these ecological resources within the
Assessment Area are also not anticipated during the operation phase.
The proposed WCPs System FS covers a large area of wetland habitats in the
Northwest New Territories. Within the proposed HHW WCP, the existing network of
pond habitats will largely be retained but zoned and managed to enhance the area’s
ecological capacity while promoting the sustainable modernisation of aquaculture
practices. Rural activities such as leisure farming may also be introduced to allow
visitors to experience a rural lifestyle and enjoy the idyllic countryside landscape
(AFCD, 2024a). The proposed HHW WCP overlaps with the current Project

Assessment Area, to the north of the ECR Alignment. The establishment of the WCP
is anticipated to improve the overall quality of the wetland habitats WCPs System
Area, including the wetland habitats at HHW WCP. The planning and design of the
ECR would be expected to be completed prior detailed planning of the HHW WCP.
Potential interface issues will be further reviewed and addressed at the detailed
studies stage as indicated in WCPs System FS (AFCD, 2024a). Cumulative impacts
on the HHW WCP within the Assessment Area are therefore not anticipated.
The “Ma Tso Lung Area and Other Sites in Kwu Tung North New Development Area
and North District – Zone 1 Ma Tso Lung Area”, will develop sites at Ma Tso Lung
area for residential and employment uses, supporting G/IC facilities, open space
and/or amenities. As the planning process for this NDA is still on-going, no definitive
design information is available at the time of preparation of this EIA. Nevertheless, it
is anticipated that the Ma Tso Lung Study would be planned to avoid recognised sites
of conservation importance as far as practicable, and that any identified impacts
would be mitigated through avoidance, minimisation and compensation.
A section of the Northern Metropolis Highway (NMH), running in a west–east direction
from Tin Shui Wai to the NTN New Town, will traverse the Ma Tso Lung area (i.e. the
Kwu Tung Section). The highway will consist of tunnel and viaduct / above-ground
sections within the Ma Tso Lung area that will branch off at Hong Kong Police Lo Wu
Range to another at-grade section aligned along the eastern portion of Ma Tso Lung
area, connecting further north to the ECR Alignment. Given the available information
at the time of preparation of this EIA, the wetlands at Hoo Hok Wai and Ma Tso Lung
San Tsuen would not be subject to direct habitat loss or disturbance from these
sections of the NMH alignment. On this basis, cumulative impacts on ecological
resources within the Assessment Area are not anticipated.
Cumulative Impact on Woodland Habitats
As described in Section 8.10.5, the Ma Tso Lung NDA project may result in the loss
of some woodland habitats. As the planning process for this NDA is still ongoing, no
definitive design information is available at the time of preparation of this EIA.
Nevertheless, it is anticipated that the Ma Tso Lung NDA studies will be planned to
avoid recognised sites of conservation importance as far as practicable, and that any
identified impacts will be mitigated through avoidance, minimisation, and
compensation measures.
The impacts of the proposed NMH to other habitats would be limited to a small portion
of woodland and mainly grassland / shrubland, located along the foothills of Crest Hill
and the existing Ma Tso Lung Road within the Assessment Area of the Project. These
habitats would be affected by at-grade section road construction and slope
stabilisation works. However, considering the affected area only supported low
diversity and abundance of fauna, and the appropriate mitigation measures would be
implemented, the cumulative ecological impacts on ecological resources within the
Assessment Area is expected to be low.
Cumulative Impact on Flight Paths
The east-west flight corridor along the LMC Meander and adjacent habitats support
major flight paths between the wetland habitats in the LMC/HHW area (on the east)
and the San Tin area (on the west). Development of the Loop was expected to have
adverse impacts to this fight corridor, which were mitigated through the provision of
the EA and associated buffer zones. As the construction of the current Project may

Mitigation of Adverse Environmental Impacts
General Principles on Mitigation Measures
According to Annex 16 of EIAO-TM and EIAO Guidance Note. 3/2010, ecological
impacts on important habitats and associated wildlife resulting from Projects should
be mitigated by, in order of priority, avoidance, minimisation, and compensation
approaches to the maximum practical extent. The proposed Project and associated
mitigation measures have been designed such that it can satisfy the requirements of
the EIAO-TM and the “no net loss in wetland” principle in Deep Bay as stipulated in
TPB PG-No.12C.
Under the current ECR alignment and its design, key ecological impacts include the
loss of wetland habitats (pond and other wetland habitats), loss of woodland habitats,
and potential impacts on flora and fauna species of conservation importance, as
discussed in Section 8.8. These impacts would require both temporary (during
construction phase) and permanent (during operation phase) mitigation. Following
the mitigation hierarchy, measures are proposed to address significant impacts to key
ecological resources, as detailed in the following sections.
Impact Avoidance Through the Preferred Project Alignment
Considerable emphasis was placed on ecological considerations under the detailed
option review process presented in Section 2.5. The selected alignment differs from
the original ECR design presented in the LMC Loop EIA, with key permanent impacts
to the pond habitats as well as fragmentation impacts at the western end of the
alignment now largely avoided through adoption of an underpass rather than open
sunken road design. Additional avoidance of wetland habitats would be achieved as
follows:-
• Considerations for the selection of construction methods are detailed in Section
2.6. The preferred ‘cut and cover’ approach will allow for reinstatement of almost
all wetland habitats including the LMC Meander, the EA and ponds habitats
along underground sections of the ECR Alignment, following completion of
construction works. While TBM tunnelling could further reduce construction
phase ecological impacts, it also has considerable drawbacks, including high
costs, environmental risks such as groundwater contamination from grouting
and bentonite, extensive land requirements for launching and retrieval shafts,
the need for a specialised workforce and equipment, and potential traffic
disruptions during TBM delivery.
• Direct impacts to the EA could be avoided if the underpass section of ECR
alignment is routed further to the north-east into the ponds of HHW, before
turning west towards the Loop. This option would however have resulted in
more extensive and prolonged overall impacts and disturbance to pond habitats
during construction phase, increasing the overall direct and indirect impacts to
wetlands. While it would affect the EA, the preferred alignment has a smaller
overall impact to wetlands
• There would be no direct impacts the OWCA Area 2.

text:
Agreement No. CE 35/2023 (HY)
Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -
Investigation, Design and Construction EIA Report
• The at-grade sections of the ECR Alignment largely follow the existing Border
Road Alignment, largely avoiding further direct impacts to wetland habitats.
• At the eastern end of the ECR Alignment, the road sections would pass to the
east of Ma Tso Lung Village, avoiding wetland habitats to the west of the Village.
By adopting this design, overall permanent impacts to wetland habitats requiring
compensation would be reduced from 3.94 ha (comprising 1.99 ha pond, 1.76 ha
freshwater marsh and 0.19 ha of seasonally wet grassland) as reported in the
previous LMC Loop EIA, to 2.09 ha (comprising 0.25 ha pond, 0.23 ha marsh and
1.61 ha of seasonally wet grassland). For high value pond habitats, permanent direct
impacts are almost wholly avoided, with the affected area would be reduced by over
87% (from 1.99 ha to 0.25 ha).
The potential extent of construction disturbance impacts is considered highly
conservative, as it does not account for phased implementation of construction works
under Phase 1, or that the majority of the construction activities will be undertaken
underground as the Alignment passes through the EA, LMC Meander and Ponds 36-
38. The area of wetland habitats temporarily impacted has increased from 7.46 ha to
9.04 ha during Phase 1 compared to the previous LMC Loop EIA. This increase is
not a result of changes to design of the ECR Alignment, but from the following factors:
• In the LMC Loop EIA, the extent of disturbance was measured from the
boundary of the permanent project alignment, whereas in the current
assessment for the Project, the disturbance extent is measured from the
Construction Area of the Project to provide a more conservative and robust
evaluation of temporary construction impact area of wetland habitats that
require compensation.
• The LMC Loop EIA did not account for temporary impacts and disturbance to
the LMC Meander.
Although temporary losses would increase, reinstatement and further enhancement
of affected areas will ensure ecological functional recovery and mitigation of residual
impacts.
The ECR Alignment would pass beneath Ping Hang Stream by means of an
underpass, thereby avoiding permanent direct impacts to this habitat.
The ECR Alignment was also designed to avoid direct impacts on the relatively
undisturbed upper sections of the Ma Tso Lung Stream. Only the already channelised
lower sections would fall within the Construction Area of the Project, and viaduct piers
would not encroach upon the stream or result in any permanent impacts.
Impact Minimisation Through Construction Phasing
A phased construction approach would be adopted to minimise prolonged and
concurrent direct and indirect impacts to wetland habitats. As described in Section
2.9, during construction, the ECR Alignment will be divided into three main sections:

Impact on Wetland Habitats
The enhancement of existing wetlands is a strategy that has been adopted by several
projects in the NWNT area (e.g. LMC Loop EIA, LMC Spur Line EIA and STLMC DN
EIA) to compensate for the direct loss of wetland habitats and indirect disturbance
impacts to the associated wildlife (especially disturbance sensitive bird species).
Enhancing the ecological function and capacity of existing habitats would
compensate for the loss or reduction of wetland areas and functional value resulting
from the Project. For example, pond habitats can be enhanced with various features
to increase function and capacity compared to typical commercially managed ponds,
thereby compensating for the loss of the functional value by accommodating a higher
abundance of wildlife. Enhancement measures could include:
• Physical modification of pond habitats to increase environmental capability;
• Managing and sequencing pond drain down across multiple ponds in the dry
season (i.e. Nov to Mar);
• Providing fencing/controlling access to reduce disturbance from human
activities and also prevent disturbance and predation of wildlife by feral dogs;

Development of the Loop: Eastern Connection Road -

To assess potential construction phase disturbance, quantitative avifauna monitoring
of all wetlands within 100m of the Construction Area of the Project should be
conducted using transect surveys. The monitoring frequency should be monthly for
12 months prior to commencement of construction and throughout the construction
period until 12 months after completion of works. The monitoring should be carried
out by qualified ecologist(s) with at least 5 years of relevant experience.
Reinstatement of the EA Zone following completion of the depressed road /
underpass sections of the ECR Alignment will be reinstated and established by the
Project Proponent / the Contractor with reference to the approved Ecological
Mitigation / Habitat Creation and Management Plan (CEDD, 2022) and the existing
as-built conditions of the EA after the completion of the aboveground works.
Monitoring of water level and quality will be carried out by the Contractor during the
construction phase. In case of non-compliance, suitable mitigation measures shall be
undertaken to meet requirement specified in Table 5.1 and Table 8.1 of CEDD (2022).
For underground reinstatement, all existing engineering and associated structures
removed during construction will be reinstated upon completion. After construction of
the underpass, the excavation cofferdam will be backfilled with compacted materials
(compacted fill or rockfill, subject to the Contractor’s design) in accordance with the
requirements of the General Specification for Civil Engineering Works published by
CEDD (CEDD, 2020). As the stone columns within the construction area will no longer
be required to support the EA and its earth bund, the relevant geotextile layers and
provisions will be reinstated to ensure that the original level of impermeability is
maintained, and native plant species will be used for reinstatement. The ecological
characteristics and function of the EA will be enhanced and maintained to a condition
no less than the existing conditions, after the reinstatement. A reinstatement and
monitoring plan for the EA would be prepared by the Contractor and submitted to
AFCD and EPD for agreement at least three months prior to commencement of
construction works.
OWCAs would be utilised as a mitigation measure for the direct and indirect impacts
during both construction and operation phases on wetland habitats under the Project.
The 3.29ha of Ponds 36-38 located outside of the Construction Area of the Project in
Area 4 would not be utilised for any construction related activities. This provides an
opportunity to enhance the ecological value of these ponds during the Phase 1
construction works. Pond habitat will be retained and, together with the remaining
area of Pond 36-38, converted into 4.38 ha ecologically enhanced pond in Area 4
upon completion of construction works in Phase 1. An updated HCMP for the OWCAs
and Area 4 would be prepared by the Contractor and submitted to AFCD and EPD
for agreement at least three months prior to commencement of construction works.
For the unavoidable loss of woodland resulting from impacts within the Construction
Area of the Project, compensatory planting has been proposed as a mitigation
measure, with the proposed location(s) and detailed design subject to further
agreement. A detailed Woodland Compensation Plan should be prepared by an
ecologist / botanist with at least 5 years relevant experience to form the basis of the
proposed compensatory planting. The mitigation plan should include implementation
details, associated management and monitoring requirements (e.g. methodology,
schedule, monitoring frequency and parameters) of the mitigation area. Upon the
completion of planting, monitoring and maintenance works (e.g., irrigation, weeding,
pruning, control of pests and diseases, replacement planting and repair of damage)
of the compensatory woodland should be implemented. The Woodland
Compensation Plan shall be submitted to the relevant authority(ies) for approval
before commencement of the compensatory planting.

Given the importance of the flight path corridor and the significance of potential
impacts, its use should be monitored to identify any effects of construction activities
focusing on the composition of bird species and their abundance using the flight path.
The flight path monitoring survey should be conducted monthly, commencing 30
minutes before sunrise and continued for at least 2 hours. The composition of bird
species and their abundance, together with the flight height and pathways of all flight
lines should be recorded.
A seasonal active night roost at the northern end of Ma Tso Lung Road was identified
within the Assessment Area. Pre-construction survey is necessary to confirm the
extent of night roost, as well as the 100m buffer area before commencement of the
construction works. The pre-construction survey shall be conducted once per month
between October to April by qualified ecologist with at least 5 years relevant
experience.
Incense trees as a species of conservation importance, should be protected as far as
practicable. As a mitigation measure, any unavoidably affected individuals should be
conserved on site or, as a last resort, transplanted to nearby suitable habitat(s) prior
to commencement of site clearance. A detailed Pre-Construction Vegetation Survey
should be carried out by a suitably qualified botanist / ecologist to identify and record
affected individuals prior to the commencement of site clearance works. A protection
and transplantation proposal, including subsequent monitoring of the affected
individuals, should be prepared and implemented by a suitably qualified ecologist /
botanist with at least 5 years relevant experience. The proposal should be submitted
to the relevant authority(ies) for approval at least one month prior to commencement
of work. Upon the transplantation of the identified individuals, a post-transplantation
monitoring should be implemented to monitor the health conditions and survival of
the transplanted individuals. Whenever transplantation is not suitable (e.g. due to
technical feasibility, poor plant health, form or structural condition), compensatory
planting for this species should be proposed. Details of post-transplantation
monitoring are provided in the standalone EM&A Manual.
Mammal species of conservation importance with high mobility (i.e. Eurasian Otter,
Small Indian Civet, Leopard Cat) should be monitored by transect survey and infrared
camera trapping. Transect count would be carried out monthly and the cameras are
suggested to be checked monthly. Pre-construction surveys for otter holts or natal
dens should be carried out in wetland habitats within 150m of the Construction Area
of the Project before the commencement of construction works. Should either be
encountered during these surveys or during construction, work in the area will cease
until the site has been inspected by an experienced ecologist. Any other mammal
species of conservation concern sighted will be reported.
A temporary aboveground wildlife crossing would be provided above the construction
area through the Ponds near Ngau Kok Shan to minimise habitat fragmentation
during construction phase. In addition, two permanent underpasses would be
provided under the at-grade road section of the ECR Alignment. The detailed design
of both aboveground wildlife crossing and underpasses would be provided in design
stage. To ensure their efficiency, monitoring of the wildlife crossing shall be
conducted during the construction phase, and underpasses shall be conducted
during the first three years upon establishment The conditions of the constructed
wildlife crossing / underpasses (e.g. structural integrity, vegetation overgrown, any
observable usage) shall be monitored every two months, while any potential usage
of the wildlife corridor by mammal species (e.g. Eurasian Otter and Small Indian Civet)

Breeding / nesting behaviour of avifauna species of conservation importance such as

Pre-construction site check for nesting activities is proposed to avoid direct injury to

Conclusion
Ecological impact assessment for the Project has been conducted following the EIA
Study Brief No. ESB-375/2025 and EIAO-TM Guidelines Annexes 8 and 16. A
detailed literature review and ecological surveys (July 2022 to December 2023) were
conducted to characterise the ecological baseline of the Assessment Area, which
extended up to 500m from the Project Boundary. Several sites of conservation
importance were identified within the Assessment Area, including the Proposed HHW
WCP, WCA, WBA, “CA”, Priority Site for Enhanced Conservation, IBA, the EA,
OWCA Area 2, off-site compensation woodland and Key Dragonfly Site in Ma Tso
Lung.
A total of 13 habitat types were identified within the Assessment Area, with wetland
habitats comprising compensatory wetland, pond, marsh, reedbed, modified
watercourse, semi-natural and natural watercourse, seasonally wet grassland; and
non-wetland habitats comprising woodland, grassland / shrubland, orchard,
plantation, agricultural land and developed land. Wetland habitats were mostly
concentrated in the northeastern portion of the Assessment Area around Hoo Hok
Wai, comprising high ecological value pond habitats, moderate to high ecological
value compensatory wetland (the EA) and semi-natural and natural watercourses
(LMC Meander), moderate ecological value marsh habitats, and low to moderate
ecological value seasonally wet grassland. Terrestrial woodland habitats were mainly
found in Horn Hill, Tse Koo Hang and Crest Hill, and are considered to be of moderate
ecological value. Flora species of conservation importance, including Incense Tree
(Aralia chinensis) and Tongue Habenaria were recorded within the Assessment Area.
Sensitive wetland habitats (i.e., compensatory wetland and ponds) in the HHW area
supported high diversity and abundance of waterbirds. Mammal species of
conservation importance, such as Leopard Cat, Small Indian Civet, and several bat
species were also recorded. While not recorded in surveys conducted specifically for
this EIA, long-term and recent records confirm the presence of Eurasian Otter in
wetland habitats of the HHW area. Other fauna of conservation importance recorded

(i.e., Metallic Cerulean, Red-breast Jezebel, Paintbrush Swift); odonate species (i.e.,
Blue Chaser, Coastal Glider); firefly species including Motschulsky’s Starworm; and
freshwater species such as the fish Gobiopterus macrolepis and freshwater crab
Somanniathelphusa zanklon and .
Direct and indirect impacts to sites of conservation importance and associated
wetland / woodland habitats and species of conservation importance would arise from
the proposed project. Compared to the design of the ECR presented in the previously
approved LMC Loop EIA (2013a), the latest design proposed in this EIA has been
developed to avoid and minimise ecological impacts as far as practicable. In particular,
key permanent impacts to the pond habitats as well as fragmentation impacts at the
western end of the alignment now largely avoided through adoption of an underpass
rather than open sunken road design. By adopting this design, the total affected
wetland habitats would be reduced by over 46 % (from 3.94 ha to 2.09 ha).
Permanent direct impacts on high value pond habitats are almost wholly avoided,
with the affected area of high ecological value pond habitats reduced by over 87%
(from 1.99 ha to 0.25 ha). The ecological characteristics and function of the portion
of the EA directly affected by the construction works will be reinstated following the
completion of works, and enhanced and maintained to a condition no less than the
existing conditions.
The provision of wetland compensation at the OWCAs already constructed as part of
the LMC Loop EIA will more than sufficiently offset unavoidable wetland impacts
arising from the construction and operation of the Project, ensuring “no net loss” in
the overall ecological function of the affected wetland habitats, in accordance with the
requirements of the EIAO-TM. Additional enhancement works of 4.38 ha of pond
habitats will be implemented at Area 4, over and above the required compensation to
further strengthen ecological functionality upon the completion of the Project. The
enhancement of Area 4 will serve to improve local ecological performance as well as
strengthen ecological linkage within the Deep Bay Wetland System, maintaining
habitat connectivity and supporting the movement of wetland-dependent fauna
through the corridor. Wetland associated avifauna species, non-avifauna species of
conservation species as well as Eurasian Otters would benefit from better water
management compared to existing abandoned and poor condition of ponds, and
more diverse and shallower sloping edge conditions to provide suitable foraging
habitat for these species. The enhanced ponds will also improve connectivity by
reinforcing the major avifaunal flight corridor traversing from Mai Po to the Loop and
HHW. In addition, the enhanced habitats would support the movement of Eurasian
Otters and other terrestrial mammals between these areas.
Aside from wetland habitats, approximately 1.68 ha of woodland will be directly
affected within the Construction Area of the Project. To comply with the requirements
of the EIAO-TM, equivalent woodland compensation will be provided on a 1:1 basis.
The location of the proposed compensatory woodland was preliminarily identified to
the southwest of the ECR Alignment. A woodland compensation plan will be
formulated and submitted prior to the commencement of construction at the woodland
habitat. With the proposed compensation measures, no unacceptable ecological
impact is anticipated to arise from the loss of habitats under the proposed
development.

used by Eurasian otters or intersecting the bird flight line will be largely confined to
restricted areas (i.e. Zones 1–3), and with the implementation of appropriate
mitigation and precautionary measures, no overlap with major flight lines or core otter
activity areas is anticipated outside the restricted zones. In addition, impacts to these
flight paths during the construction phase are expected to be minimal considering no
above-ground structures exceeding 15m above the existing ground level be
established in this area. No operation phase impacts are expected. Time and
seasonal restriction will be adopted for any aboveground noisy construction activities
(with the use of PME) within sensitive wetland area that fall within the Construction
Area of the Project, permitted only between 0900h to 1700h throughout the year,
unless a cover is provided to create the fully enclosed conditions. This restriction is
intended to avoid the time of day when flight lines and otters are most active in the
region.

recorded within the Construction Area of the Project. A detailed vegetation survey
should be conducted prior to the commencement of construction works to identify
potentially affected plant individuals. All identified individuals would be labelled and
fenced off on-site for better preservation, or in the case of unavoidable direct impacts,
for transplantation or seedling planting according to the Protection and
Transplantation / Seedling Planting Proposal.

Chinese bullfrog; one freshwater crab species, Somanniathelphusa zanklon; and one
freshwater fish species, Gobiopterus macrolepis) were recorded within or close to
Construction Area of the Project, as well as actual / suspected breeding of three
avifauna species of conservation importance (White-throated Kingfisher, Chinese
Francolin and Eurasian Eagle Owl). Due to the low mobility of these species and/or

construction surveys should be conducted for these species, followed by

operation. During the construction phase, works would be divided into three large
sections (Sections 1,2,3), to be completed in two phases (Sections 1 and 3 and
Sections 2 and 3). All works would be completed at Section 1 before any works
commence at Section 2, minimising disturbance and fragmentation impacts. Within
the most sensitive wetland area (i.e., the EA, LMC Meander and ponds 36 - 38),
works would be further phased to ensure some areas of intact habitat are maintained
at all times, and a temporary aboveground wildlife crossing (approximately 40m)
would be installed to ensure connectivity is maintained during construction phase.
Habitats in this area would be reinstated following completion of construction works,
avoiding long-term fragmentation impacts. Two permanent wildlife underpasses
would be incorporated in the at-grade section of ECR Alignment, linking the wooded
habitat at Tse Koo Hang to the south with wetland habitats at Hoo Hok Wai to the
north. These wildlife underpasses would facilitate ecological linkage, allowing
movement of non-flying mammals and terrestrial herpetofauna.
A range of mitigation measures as well as general good site practises have been
proposed to reduce the disturbance impacts (e.g. noise, glare and dust) and water
quality impacts on habitats, sites of conservation importance and wildlife during the
construction phase. The operational impact would be largely avoided through the
design of the ECR Alignment, and the proposed underpasses with solid parapet, as
well as noise and lighting management as precautionary measures, which further
reduce habitat fragmentation associated with the at-grade sections of the ECR and
other potential indirect impacts during the operation phase.
With the implementation of the aforementioned mitigation measures, no
unacceptable impacts are anticipated to arise from the construction or operation of
the Project on ecological resources recorded within the Project Assessment Area.
